articles.title: Energiebranche: CX schlägt den günstigsten Tarif
articles.text:
Was entscheidet, ob ein Energiekunde bleibt – wenn nicht der Preis?
Der Wettbewerb verlagert sich
Es war lange Zeit eine einfache Gleichung: Wer den günstigsten Tarif anbietet, gewinnt den Kunden. Wer ihn günstig hält, behält ihn. Diese Logik hat die Energiebranche über Jahre geprägt, doch sie greift immer weniger.
Tarife werden transparenter, Vergleichsportale mächtiger, Anbieterwechsel reibungsloser. Was einmal Kunden gehalten hat, verliert an Wirkung. Der Preis bleibt relevant. Aber er reicht nicht mehr aus, um eine Kundenbeziehung zu tragen.
Was bleibt, wenn der Tarif sich nicht mehr unterscheidet? Die Erfahrung, die ein Unternehmen hinterlässt. Die Art, wie es kommuniziert, wenn etwas nicht stimmt. Wie es sich anfühlt, ein Anliegen zu klären und eine Antwort zu bekommen, die wirklich weiterhilft. Customer Experience ist kein Servicethema. Sie ist die Frage, womit Energieunternehmen künftig noch unverwechselbar sind.
Jede Interaktion prägt die Marke
Was Kunden über ein Energieunternehmen denken, entsteht selten in großen Momenten, sondern in den alltäglichen Interaktionen, von denen es mehr gibt, als man zunächst vermuten würde. Ob eine Anfrage schnell und verständlich gelöst wird, ob Kommunikation proaktiv kommt oder ob Self-Service-Angebote wirklich funktionieren: Jeder dieser Kontaktpunkte ist eine stille Entscheidung. Vertrauen aufbauen oder abbauen, Bindung stärken oder schwächen.
In einem Markt, in dem der nächste Anbieter nur einen Klick entfernt ist, summieren sich diese Momente schneller, als es Preismodelle ausgleichen können. Wer seine Customer Journey deshalb nur als Abfolge von Prozessen betrachtet, die es zu optimieren gilt, denkt zu kurz. Es geht um Momente, die eine Marke prägen und darüber entscheiden, ob ein Kunde bleibt, wechselt oder weiterempfiehlt.
Warum Kundenbindung sich rechnet und Wechsel teuer ist
Wer Kundenbindung als weiches Ziel betrachtet, unterschätzt ihren wirtschaftlichen Wert. Ein Kunde, der bleibt, ist nicht nur gesicherter Umsatz. Er ist vermiedener Akquisitionsaufwand, ein stabilerer Planungshorizont und ein potenzieller Multiplikator.
Umgekehrt gilt: Wechsel ist teuer. Nicht nur wegen der Kosten für Neukundengewinnung, sondern weil abwandernde Kunden oft in Momenten gehen, in denen eine bessere Erfahrung sie hätte halten können. Schlechte Serviceerlebnisse, fehlende Transparenz bei Preisanpassungen, ungelöste Anliegen: Das sind keine Zufälle, sondern vermeidbare Verluste.
Die Verbindung aus Markenerlebnis und wirtschaftlichem Wert ist damit keine weiche These, sondern eine unternehmerische Entscheidung. Wer in die Qualität der Kundenbeziehung investiert, investiert in die Stabilität seines Geschäftsmodells, gerade in einem Markt, der sich strukturell weiter liberalisiert.
Technologie und KI als Gestaltungsmittel, nicht als Selbstzweck
Hier kommt Technologie ins Spiel, aber anders, als sie oft diskutiert wird. KI ist in der Energiebranche kein Differenzierungsmerkmal mehr: über 80 Prozent der KI-Anbieter für die Energiewirtschaft sind mittlerweile branchenspezialisiert, 2024 waren es erst 60 Prozent. Entscheidend ist, was Unternehmen daraus machen. Denn nicht die Technologie selbst schafft Unverwechselbarkeit, sondern die Frage, wo und wie sie eingesetzt wird.
Wer Technologie primär als Kostenhebel betrachtet, optimiert Teilbereiche und tut damit genau das, was aktuell 36 Prozent der Energieunternehmen tun, die im größten KI-Nutzen vor allem Effizienzgewinne sehen, während nur 22 Prozent auf das Kundenerlebnis zielen. Wer sie als Gestaltungsmittel für Kundenerlebnisse begreift, verändert die Beziehung zur Marke. Der Unterschied liegt nicht in der Technologie selbst, sondern in der Frage, mit der man anfängt. „Wie reduzieren wir Kontaktvolumen?“ führt zu einem anderen Ergebnis als: „Wie stellen wir sicher, dass Kunden in kritischen Momenten die Erfahrung machen, die sie bindet?“ Beide Fragen können zur selben Lösung führen, aber nur die zweite baut eine Marke.
Proaktive Kommunikation, intuitive Self-Service-Angebote, KI-gestützte Erkennung von Abwanderungsrisiken, bevor ein Kunde kündigt: Das sind keine reinen Effizienzmaßnahmen, sondern Markenerlebnisse. Und sie entstehen nur, wenn Technologie von Anfang an im Dienst der Kundenbindung gedacht wird, nicht umgekehrt.
Eine positive Customer Journey entscheidet über den weiteren Prozess der Kundenbindung. (Bild: Getty Images)
Warum das Zusammendenken entscheidet
Der häufigste Grund, warum CX-Initiativen in der Energiebranche hinter ihren Möglichkeiten bleiben, ist nicht fehlende Ambition, sondern fehlende Verbindung.
Wenn CX-Strategie, Technologieprojekte und operative Umsetzung in getrennten Verantwortlichkeiten laufen, entstehen Reibungsverluste, die sich im Kundenerlebnis zeigen, auch wenn jeder Bereich für sich funktioniert. Prozesse sind optimiert, aber nicht verbunden. Lösungen sind implementiert, aber nicht integriert. Kommunikation ist geplant, aber operativ nicht skalierbar.
Die Antwort auf die Frage, was ein Energieunternehmen künftig unverwechselbar macht, lässt sich nicht in einer Abteilung entwickeln. Sie entsteht, wenn Customer Experience, Technologie und Operations gemeinsam auf dasselbe Ziel ausgerichtet sind: eine Kundenbeziehung, die hält.
Erfahrung, die zählt
Concentrix begleitet Energieunternehmen im DACH-Raum und weltweit durch genau diesen Prozess. Was Concentrix dabei einbringt, ist ein Ansatz, der Kompetenzen vereint, die in der Praxis selten in einer Hand liegen: die strategische Perspektive eines Consultants, die technische Umsetzungsstärke eines Integrators und die operative Verlässlichkeit eines langfristigen Outsourcing-Partners. Verbunden mit tiefem Branchenwissen und echter Expertise in Customer Experience und Enterprise-Prozessen.
Dieser Ansatz ermöglicht es, nicht nur zu beraten oder zu implementieren, sondern Verantwortung über den gesamten Prozess zu übernehmen: von der ersten strategischen Frage bis in den laufenden Betrieb. Und genau das ist der Unterschied, der darüber entscheidet, ob aus einer CX-Initiative ein Kundenerlebnis wird, das wirklich hält.
Folge Concentrix auf LinkedIn für weitere Perspektiven zu CX, KI und Transformation in der Energiebranche.
Was künftig unverwechselbar macht
Tarife werden sich weiter angleichen, Wechsel werden einfacher werden. Was bleibt, ist die Frage, welche Erfahrung ein Energieunternehmen hinterlässt. Unternehmen, die das heute als strategische Frage begreifen, bauen einen Vorsprung auf, den kein Preismodell schnell einholt.
Mehr aus Customer Experience machen
Wie Customer Experience in der Energiebranche konkret wirkt und welche Leitfragen Entscheider dabei leiten sollten, zeigt der Concentrix-Blog: Warum der günstigste Tarif den Klick gewinnt, aber nicht die Beziehung

articles.title: Speaker-labeled transcription with WhisperX on SageMaker AI | Amazon Web Services
articles.text:
Artificial Intelligence
Speaker-labeled transcription with WhisperX on SageMaker AI
Any team working with spoken audio hits the same wall with generic speech-to-text. Think contact-center calls, all-hands meetings, podcasts, depositions, and broadcast media. These workloads need two things that standard transcription gets wrong. First, timestamps land at the utterance level, off by several seconds. Second, there’s no reliable answer to “who said what.” Those gaps make transcripts hard to search, caption, redact, or analyze at scale. A missing speaker label breaks compliance review, and an imprecise timestamp breaks a caption or a redaction.
WhisperX closes both gaps. It wraps OpenAI’s Whisper with batched inference, adds wav2vec2 forced alignment for precise per-word timestamps, and adds speaker diarization to label who spoke. These capabilities map directly to real workloads. Contact centers can measure talk time, check script adherence, and run sentiment analysis, while teams turn meetings into searchable notes. Media and e-learning teams generate accurate captions (in SubRip Subtitle (SRT) and Web Video Text Tracks (VTT) format) for large content libraries. Time-sensitive uses get text the moment someone speaks. In regulated fields like healthcare, legal, and finance, speaker-labeled transcripts support audits and legal discovery.
The AWS WhisperX Deep Learning Container (DLC) packages all of this into a GPU-ready image. You deploy it to an Amazon SageMaker AI real-time or asynchronous endpoint without building a custom image. In this post, we show how to deploy both endpoint types and when to choose each. We also cover the production details that matter: the GPU AMI pin, scaling, Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) setup, and cost controls. This post is part of a multimodal series showcasing specialized AWS DLCs. The series spans three AWS DLCs across four use cases: (1) vLLM-Omni for text-to-speech, (2) vLLM-Omni for image and video, (3) WhisperX for speech-to-text (this post), and (4) llama.cpp.
What is WhisperX, and what workloads it unlocks
Whisper is a popular open source automatic speech recognition (ASR) model family from OpenAI that transcribes spoken audio into text accurately across many languages. It focuses on high-quality transcription and produces timestamps at the phrase or segment level. WhisperX is an open source project that builds on Whisper and extends it for production workloads. It adds per-word timestamps, speaker labels, and faster transcription, three capabilities that together turn raw audio into structured, analyzable transcripts.
Why a purpose-built Deep Learning Container
The AWS WhisperX DLC is a maintained, GPU-ready image that already contains Whisper, the alignment models, and the diarization weights, with no Hugging Face token required. It follows the standard Amazon SageMaker AI serving contract, so you deploy it like any other model.
- Serving contract: The container serves on port 8080 and exposesPOST /invocations for inference andGET /ping for health checks.
- Request format: The endpoint expects multipart/form-data , with the audio as thefile part plus optional string fields such aslanguage ,diarize , andresponse_format . Amazon SageMaker AI passes theContentType header (including the multipart boundary) through to the container unchanged.
- Output formats: json ,verbose_json ,srt , andvtt , so the same endpoint feeds analytics pipelines and video editors alike.
Choosing between real-time and asynchronous endpoints
Amazon SageMaker AI supports both real-time and asynchronous endpoints, so you can serve the same WhisperX DLC through either pattern. The decision usually comes down to clip length and interactivity. For long audio, use the asynchronous endpoint: it’s the recommended path when transcription, alignment, and diarization need more time to run. Reserve the real-time endpoint for short, interactive clips that finish within the Amazon SageMaker AI 60-second response cap.
| Dimension | Real-time endpoint | Asynchronous endpoint | 
| Best for | Short, interactive clips | Long audio, high-volume batch | 
| Latency | Synchronous, must finish < 60s | Submit-and-poll. No response cap | 
| Invocation | InvokeEndpoint (inline body) | InvokeEndpointAsync (S3 reference) | 
| I/O | Body in request / response | Input + output in Amazon S3 | 
| Scaling | Add instances (one request/container) | Add instances. Can autoscale to zero | 
| Cost profile | Bills while endpoint is up | Scale-to-zero when idle saves cost | 
Solution architecture
Both patterns share the same container contract. Amazon SageMaker AI forwards each request to the WhisperX DLC on port 8080. The real-time pattern is synchronous, and the asynchronous pattern brokers input and output through Amazon S3. Instance selection (ml.g4dn.xlarge for cost, ml.g5.2xlarge for headroom) and the required GPU AMI pin apply to both, and you scale throughput by adding instances rather than concurrency. The request/response sequence for each endpoint type is shown in its walkthrough section.
Prerequisites
- An AWS account and an Amazon SageMaker AI execution role that can create_model ,create_endpoint , and (for asynchronous inference) read and write S3.
- GPU service quota for your endpoint instance type (for example, ml.g4dn.xlarge orml.g5.2xlarge ).
- The WhisperX DLC image URI from Amazon Elastic Container Registry (Amazon ECR) (for example, 763104351884.dkr.ecr.<region>.amazonaws.com/whisperx:3.8.6-cu128-amzn2023-sagemaker ).
- For asynchronous inference, an S3 bucket whose name contains “sagemaker.” The default AmazonSageMakerFullAccess policy grants S3 access only to such buckets.
A complete, runnable JupyterLab notebook that walks through these steps end to end is available in the AWS Samples repository. You can run it in Amazon SageMaker AI Studio against your own audio.
Walkthrough: Real-time endpoint
The real-time endpoint returns the transcript in the same synchronous call. Use it for short clips that comfortably finish within the 60-second cap. Figure 1 is a sequence diagram that traces a single real-time request end to end, from the client call through in-container transcription to the inline transcript.
Reading the sequence end to end: the client assembles a multipart/form-data body (the audio as the file part plus fields such as language, diarize, and word-level timestamp granularity) and calls InvokeEndpoint. Amazon SageMaker AI forwards the request to the container on port 8080, passing the ContentType and its multipart boundary through unchanged. Inside the container, WhisperX runs voice-activity detection and batched Whisper transcription, wav2vec2 forced alignment for per-word timestamps, and speaker diarization to label who is speaking. It then serializes the result. The runtime returns the transcript (segments, words with timestamps, and speaker labels) inline to the client, which must complete within the Amazon SageMaker AI 60-second response cap.
Create the model and endpoint config
Register the WhisperX DLC as a model, where IMAGE_URI points at the WhisperX DLC in Amazon ECR, then create an endpoint config. On every GPU variant, you must set InferenceAmiVersion to al2-ami-sagemaker-inference-gpu-3-1. Without this pin, the endpoint fails to start with a zero-log CannotStartContainerError. Allow a generous startup health-check timeout because the weights load lazily.
Invoke with diarization and word timestamps
Build a multipart/form-data body with the audio as the file part and fields such as language=en, diarize=true, and response_format=verbose_json. The response contains segments, per-word timestamps, and speaker labels.
The example GitHub repository uses a public-domain recording of the air traffic control (ATC) communications from US Airways Flight 1549, the 2009 “Miracle on the Hudson” emergency landing. It’s a real multi-party radio exchange with background noise, radio compression, and rapid callsign and frequency readouts. Those conditions make it a strong test of transcription accuracy, word-level timestamps, and speaker diarization. The full approximately 3-minute recording is sent to the asynchronous endpoint, and a 40-second segment to the real-time endpoint.
Running this against a 40-second segment of the source audio returns the following diarized, word-timed transcript:
Walkthrough: Asynchronous endpoint
The asynchronous endpoint removes the 60-second cap and is the recommended path for long audio. Input and output are brokered through Amazon S3, and you poll for the result. Figure 2 is a sequence diagram that traces the full asynchronous lifecycle, from the S3 upload and InvokeEndpointAsync call through container processing to the S3 output and failure paths.
Reading the sequence end to end: the client uploads the multipart body to Amazon S3 and calls InvokeEndpointAsync with the object’s InputLocation. It receives an OutputLocation and FailureLocation immediately rather than waiting for the transcript. Amazon SageMaker AI reads the input from Amazon S3 and forwards it to the container on port 8080. There, the same voice-activity detection, batched transcription, forced-alignment, and diarization pipeline runs, one request per container. On success, the container writes the transcript to the S3 output path, or an error document to the failure path. The client polls the output path for the result and checks the failure path, so a failed job surfaces an error instead of looping indefinitely. Because work is brokered through Amazon S3, this path isn’t bound by the 60-second cap and suits long audio.
Create the asynchronous endpoint config
The only structural difference from the real-time endpoint is the endpoint config: it adds an AsyncInferenceConfig with an S3 OutputPath and S3FailurePath. Set MaxConcurrentInvocationsPerInstance=1 to match the container’s single-worker limit, and keep the same InferenceAmiVersion pin. IMAGE_URI is the same WhisperX DLC used for the real-time endpoint.
The rest of the workflow is identical to the real-time walkthrough. Building the multipart/form-data request (the build_multipart helper and transcription fields) is unchanged. You submit it with invoke_endpoint_async by S3 reference instead of invoke_endpoint, then read the transcript from the OutputLocation and check the FailureLocation. Cleanup is also the same.
Submitting the full approximately 3-minute recording to the asynchronous endpoint returns the following transcript (first and last five lines shown):
Cleaning up
A GPU endpoint bills continuously until you delete it. When you are done, delete the endpoint, endpoint config, and model for both endpoints, and remove any S3 input and output artifacts you no longer need.
Best practices and production considerations
- Pin the GPU AMI – Always set InferenceAmiVersion=al2-ami-sagemaker-inference-gpu-3-1 on GPU variants. The default host AMI ships drivers that fail to start this CUDA 12.8 image.
- Scale by instances, not concurrency – Inference is serialized to one request per container. Set MaxConcurrentInvocationsPerInstance=1 on asynchronous endpoints and add instances or containers for throughput.
- Autoscale asynchronous endpoints to zero – For bursty batch workloads, scale the asynchronous endpoint to zero instances when idle to cut cost, and use Amazon Simple Notification Service (Amazon SNS) completion notifications instead of tight polling.
- Right-size the GPU, and use instance pools for availability – Use ml.g4dn.xlarge (T4) for cost orml.g5.2xlarge (A10G) for headroom. To avoid insufficient-capacity errors, list up to five instance types in an Amazon SageMaker AI instance pool. It provisions the highest-priority type first and falls back automatically when capacity is unavailable.
- Secure the S3 artifacts – Turn on S3 Block Public Access, default SSE-S3 or SSE-KMS encryption, and BucketOwnerEnforced ownership on the asynchronous bucket. Scope the execution role to specific buckets and keys.
- Handle personally identifiable information (PII) responsibly – Transcripts of calls and meetings might contain sensitive data, so encrypt artifacts, restrict access, and apply redaction downstream using the word-level timestamps.
- Observe and retry – Monitor with Amazon CloudWatch, alarm on failures, and retry around the cold-start behavior described earlier. For deeper GPU and inference visibility, turn on the Amazon SageMaker AI detailed metrics and Insights dashboard on CloudWatch.
Conclusion
In this post, we showed how to deploy the AWS WhisperX Deep Learning Container to Amazon SageMaker AI for word-level, speaker-labeled transcription. We used a real-time endpoint for short interactive clips and an asynchronous endpoint for long, high-volume audio. We covered the production details that matter most: the required GPU AMI pin, single-request-per-container scaling, S3 bucket naming, and cost controls.
To go further, explore the WhisperX DLC deployment guide, review Amazon SageMaker AI asynchronous inference, and try the accompanying demo notebook against your own audio. You can also find the full working example in the AWS Samples GitHub repository.
Acknowledgements
The authors thank the AWS Deep Learning Containers and Amazon SageMaker AI teams for their technical review and contributions to the sample.

articles.title: Meta Connect 2026, everything Meta announced including Muse
articles.text:
Table of contents
Meta Connect 2026 took place on September 23 and 24 at Meta’s headquarters in Menlo Park, California, where Mark Zuckerberg unveiled new smart glasses, a lighter VR headset, and a small device designed to work with Muse, Meta’s AI agent.
Meta also introduced its first smart glasses without a camera, as concerns grow about people being recorded without their knowledge by camera-equipped glasses. The new glasses remove the camera but retain microphones and can still connect to Meta’s AI services.
If you live in Africa, you also want to know which of these devices you can buy at home. This article covers every big announcement, prices, release dates, and what you can expect in your country.
Everything Meta announced at Meta Connect 2026
Here is a quick look at each device’s price and release date.
| Product | Starting price | Availability | 
|---|---|---|
| Ray-Ban Meta Gen 3 | $449 | On sale now in supported markets | 
| Ray-Ban Meta Audio | $349 | Pre-orders open; ships October 13 | 
| Meta Adventurer | $249 | Pre-orders open; on sale October 23 | 
| Meta Glasses LISA Edition | $399 | Announced; check your local store | 
| Meta VR Glasses | $1,299.99 | Spring 2027 | 
| Muse Charm | Not announced | Release date not announced | 
These are Meta’s US prices. Prices in your country may be different.
1. Ray-Ban Meta Gen 3
Ray-Ban Meta Gen 3 starts at $449 and is on sale now in markets where Meta sells its glasses. It replaces the Gen 2 model from 2025. Here is what changes:
- Slimmer frames and adjustable temple tips for a better fit
- Up to nine hours of battery life, one hour more than Gen 2
- A new action button that opens Meta AI fast, so you can skip saying “Hey Meta” on a quiet train
- Six microphones that Meta says block more than 90% of background noise on calls
The camera stays the same. You still get 12-megapixel photos and 3K video.
Gen 3 comes in 27 frame-and-lens combinations, including the new Aviator and Zena cat-eye frames alongside the classic Wayfarer. A limited-edition Aviator Connect model starts at $579. That is $70 more than the Gen 2’s launch price, according to Gear Live.
2. The LISA edition
Meta teamed up with BLACKPINK star LISA on two frames: Adventurer LISA Edition and Capri LISA Edition. Both start at $399. You get:
- Star details on the frames
- A special case
- Case charms based on her pets
- Digital photocards you unlock with the glasses
These frames are part of the Meta Glasses range. They are separate from the Ray-Ban Meta Gen 3.
3. Ray-Ban Meta Audio
Ray-Ban Meta Audio is Meta’s first pair of audio glasses. Open-ear speakers let you play music, take calls, listen to podcasts, and chat with Meta AI. The glasses have no camera, so they cannot take photos or record video.
This is Meta’s clearest answer to people uneasy about camera glasses. Some privacy questions remain. The glasses still have microphones, and your voice requests still go to an AI service.
- Weight: 43 grams
- Battery: up to 12 hours per charge, plus up to 48 more hours from the case
- Frames: Clubmaster and Burbank, with 23 colour and lens combinations
- Price and date: from $349, pre-orders open now, ships October 13
4. Meta VR Glasses
Meta VR Glasses look like thick glasses instead of a strapped headset. They weigh about 100 grams. Meta says that makes them five times lighter than Quest 3.
Meta gets there by splitting the device in two. The glasses hold the displays and sensors. A small puck holds the processor and battery, and it also stores your apps. An optical cable links the glasses to the puck, which you can clip to your pocket or set on a table.
Meta VR Glasses cost $1,299.99 and arrive in spring 2027.
How you control them
You control the glasses with your eyes and hand gestures. Voice commands work too. Controllers are optional.
- More than 75 games work with hand gestures at launch
- Touch Plus controllers work for games that need them
- A Bluetooth gamepad works with Xbox Cloud Gaming
- Beat Saber gets a new hand-tracking mode called Flux next spring, on both VR Glasses and Quest
Work and entertainment
For work, you can open several virtual screens at once. Meta says your desk can act as a keyboard and touchpad. You can also connect a Mac or Windows PC.
For fun, Meta lined up streaming and sports partners. You also get immersive versions of Avengers: Infinity War and Star Wars: A New Hope. Some films and sports streams depend on your country and your subscriptions.
Hologram calls
Meta also showed a feature it calls hologram. You scan your face with your phone, and Meta builds a lifelike digital version of you. It copies your face and expressions live during calls. It comes to Meta VR Glasses at launch. Meta Ray-Ban Display users in the US get early access on WhatsApp first.
5. Muse Charm
Muse Charm is a small, pocket-sized gadget for talking to Muse. It uses Muse’s live voice model, so you speak to it the way you speak on a phone call.
Meta showed Muse Charm on stage but shared few details. It has not announced a price or a release date and says it will share more later this year.
Tom’s Guide reports that the device has a fingerprint sensor on its edge and works without a phone. The outlet also reports that Zuckerberg wants it out in time for the holidays. Meta has not confirmed these details, so treat them as early reports.
6. Muse, Meta’s AI agent
What Muse does
Meta launched Muse on September 8, two weeks before Connect. Muse can open websites, fill forms, plan trips, and shop for you. It asks for your approval before sensitive steps, like sending an email or paying for something. Muse runs inside its own protected virtual computer, which Meta calls Muse Secure VM.
Shopping, travel and work tools
Meta added new connections so Muse can do more for you:
- Shopping: Walmart, Best Buy, Sephora, Ulta, Wayfair, Gap and Fanatics
- Payments: Shop Pay and PayPal, on top of Stripe’s Link, which Muse already supported
- Travel and groceries: Expedia for trips and Instacart for grocery orders
- Work: Notion, Granola, GitHub and Box
Check that a service works in your country before you rely on it. Meta’s list does not promise that every partner works everywhere.
Muse on Mac and on your glasses
Muse for Mac can now use the apps on your computer, with your permission. You can give it a list of tasks, walk away, and it keeps working.
On supported AI glasses, Muse will answer to its name and help with whatever you are looking at. Meta says this arrives in the next few months. It has not shared dates for each model or country.
A custom voice and face
You can describe the voice you want Muse to have, including how fast it talks and its accent. Meta also announced a live avatar that gives Muse an expressive face on screen. Muse also gets its own email address.
7. New features for Meta glasses
Hearing enhancement
Meta announced FDA-cleared software that helps adults with mild to moderate hearing loss. It arrives in the US later this year on supported glasses. You pay $149.99 to add it, or you get it with a Meta One subscription. Meta has not said if the $149.99 is a yearly fee.
Better maps on Meta Ray-Ban Display
Meta Ray-Ban Display gets cycling and public transit directions later this month in the US and Canada. Early access to hologram calls on Display comes to the US in the coming months. Meta also opened online orders for Display and started selling it in more countries outside the US.
Private Processing and camera tools
Meta says Private Processing is coming to its AI glasses. It lets some AI requests run without Meta seeing your data. Meta also announced new camera tools, including dynamic photos and Dolby Atmos video capture later on. Meta has not shared one rollout date for all these features.
Other Meta Connect 2026 announcements
- Meta Adventurer: Meta’s cheapest Meta Glasses yet. It pairs a black frame with grey lenses and ships with a plug-in case. It costs $249 and goes on sale October 23 in all countries where Meta Glasses are sold
- New frames: Capri and Nova frames join the range. A limited Meta Fury edition with a clear frame and mirrored lenses sells only at Connect and Meta Lab stores at launch
- Mix & Match: a new US programme that lets you build your own pair
- More styles: Meta says it will offer more than 100 glasses options across its brands by the end of 2026
Meta’s event recap does not include a new Quest headset.
Detailed specs
These are the specs Meta has confirmed so far.
Display
- Meta VR Glasses: micro-OLED 5K Infinite Display
- Meta VR Glasses: 37 pixels per degree
- Meta VR Glasses: Dolby Vision support
- Ray-Ban Meta Gen 3 and Ray-Ban Meta Audio: no display
Processor
- Meta VR Glasses: Qualcomm Snapdragon Reality Elite, housed in the puck
- Ray-Ban Meta Gen 3 and Ray-Ban Meta Audio: Meta has not named the chip
Battery and charging
- Ray-Ban Meta Gen 3: up to 9 hours
- Ray-Ban Meta Audio: up to 12 hours, plus up to 48 hours from the case
- Meta VR Glasses: up to 3 hours of high-resolution media playback
- Meta VR Glasses: 45W charging on the puck
Camera
- Ray-Ban Meta Gen 3: 12MP photos and 3K video
- Ray-Ban Meta Audio: no camera
Audio and microphones
- Ray-Ban Meta Gen 3: six microphones that cut more than 90% of background noise
- Meta VR Glasses: Dolby Atmos audio
Weight
- Ray-Ban Meta Audio: 43 grams
- Meta VR Glasses: about 100 grams for the glasses
Some spec sheets online list the VR Glasses’ per-eye resolution, plus RAM, storage size, and puck weight. Meta has not confirmed those numbers yet.
Will the new glasses come to Nigeria, Kenya and South Africa?
South Africa
Meta names South Africa among 12 new markets getting Ray-Ban Meta and Oakley Meta glasses later in 2026. Ray-Ban Meta Optics is on the list too.
Meta has not shared a local date or price. It also has not promised South Africa the new Audio glasses or the VR Glasses, and Muse Charm has no launch market yet.
Nigeria and Kenya
Meta has not announced a launch in Nigeria or Kenya for any of these devices. You may find imported units from sellers on Jumia, Konga, Jiji, or Slot. Before you pay, check these four things:
- The exact model and generation
- Warranty cover
- Which AI features work in your country
- The seller’s return policy
Naira and shilling prices move with exchange rates and import costs. The price you see this week may change next week.
Features with country limits
Some features only work in certain countries for now:
- Hearing enhancement: US only
- Hologram calls on Display: US early access
- Cycling and transit directions on Display: US and Canada
- Muse shopping partners: mostly US stores
If you live in Lagos, Accra, Nairobi, or Johannesburg, wait for local support details before you pay for a device because of these features.
True scale demands moving beyond surface-level integrations to robust execution. We’ve filtered the noise out of Moonshot 2026, optimising the conference strictly for high-calibre connections between startup founders, global financial operators, enterprise leaders and individuals rewiring Africa’s technical frameworks. Get 20% off Early Bird tickets for a limited time.

articles.title: Nubank acaba com mais um benefício gratuito • Tecnoblog
articles.text:
Nubank acaba com mais um benefício gratuito
Ao mesmo tempo, Ultravioleta cria seguro contra fraudes cibernéticas e roubo de itens pessoais.
Resumo
- O Nubank encerrou o seguro gratuito de compras não reconhecidas para clientes Ultravioleta e lançou o Ultravioleta Protegido, com custo de R$ 19,99 por mês.
- O novo seguro oferece coberturas como golpes digitais e roubo de itens pessoais, com limites de até R$ 30 mil e R$ 7,5 mil, respectivamente.
- A mudança gerou críticas, com clientes reclamando da perda de um benefício gratuito e do aumento de custos associados ao cartão Ultravioleta.
Os clientes do Nubank sofreram um revés que vai pesar no bolso: a empresa acabou com o seguro gratuito de compras não reconhecidas que fazia parte dos benefícios do cartão de alta renda Ultravioleta. Ao mesmo tempo, passou a oferecer o seguro Ultravioleta Protegido, que é mais completo, mas custa R$ 19,99 por mês. Ou seja, os consumidores que quiserem esse tipo de proteção terão um custo adicional que chega a R$ 239,88 por ano.
A mudança (com razão) gerou críticas na internet. Algumas pessoas apontaram que o serviço anterior, chamado de Proteção de Transações Digitais, era citado até mesmo nos termos e condições do programa Ultravioleta.
O que mudou no Ultravioleta?
Nós procuramos o Nubank para entender a situação. Em resposta ao Tecnoblog, o banco enfatizou que são produtos distintos e que este novo seguro é resultado “de uma escuta ativa” das necessidades dos clientes, que apontaram “golpes, fraudes digitais e roubo de itens pessoais entre os incidentes que mais geram preocupação”.
Segundo o comunicado, o Ultravioleta Protegido reúne duas coberturas:
- Golpes digitais, uso forçado do cartão e transferências sob ameaça – até R$ 30 mil, com limite de quatro acionamentos por ano
- Bolsa Protegida – até R$ 7,5 mil em caso de roubo de bolsa ou mochila com celular, notebook e outros itens pessoais
A contratação pode ser feita diretamente no app do Nubank. Já o acionamento da cobertura do seguro deve ocorrer pelo SAC, também no app, que está disponível 24 horas por dia. O banco afirma que 98% dos reembolsos são pagos em até cinco dias úteis.
Como condição de lançamento, por tempo limitado, quem contratá-lo recebe 50% do valor de volta em cashback nos três primeiros meses.
“Os clientes também contam com o Atendimento Ultravioleta 24 horas, e as demais soluções de segurança do Nubank, como o Modo Rua, permanecem disponíveis.”
Benefícios viraram cobranças
Em uma publicação na comunidade oficial, o cliente Renê Fraga reconhece que o novo seguro traz coberturas mais completas, como a da bolsa, mas critica o modelo: “algo que era uma vantagem do Ultravioleta agora tem preço separado”. Na avaliação dele, o banco está retirando benefícios e transformando serviços gratuitos em produtos à parte, enquanto o custo para manter o cartão sobe.
A implementação do novo Ultravioleta Protegido ocorre ao longo de setembro. Já o antigo Proteção de Transações Digitais será encerrado até outubro.
Essa não é a primeira mudança do tipo. A assinatura gratuita do Rappi Pro deixou de existir em dezembro de 2024. Já em setembro de 2025, o Nubank encerrou o cashback com rendimento de 200% do CDI, o que levou a um sem-número de reclamações. Na mesma reformulação, a mensalidade do Ultravioleta subiu de R$ 49 para R$ 89 e o gasto mínimo para isenção passou de R$ 5 mil para R$ 8 mil por mês no crédito. A gratuidade permanece para quem tem R$ 50 mil guardados ou investidos.
A HBO Max também mudou. Em abril, o Nubank anunciou o fim do acesso gratuito ao streaming e, em julho, revisou a decisão. Os clientes atuais têm 12 meses do plano Básico com Anúncios sem custo e, depois disso, pagam R$ 4,90 por mês – sejamos sinceros, um valor ainda abaixo do habitual. Na ocasião, eles disseram que as alterações nos benefícios seguem as condições de mercado e o nível de adoção dos clientes.
Nesta quarta-feira (23/09), o Nubank apresentou a nova versão de seu programa de pontos. O NuCoin estreia níveis, sorteios e descontos, e é válido apenas para adeptos do cartão Roxinho (Croma e Ultravioleta ficam de fora).

articles.title: Jogo grátis na Epic Games: Astrea Six Sided Oracles e Mechabellum
articles.text:
Toda semana você encontra pelo menos um jogo grátis na Epic Games Store para baixar. Nesta semana, Astrea: Six Sided Oracles é um jogo indie que tem uma proposta bem diferenciada para um roguelike, enquanto Mechabellum é um jogo de estratégia com robôs gigantes e foco no multiplayer — disponíveis de 24 de setembro a 01 de outubro.
Astrea: Six Sided Oracles
Astrea: Six Sided Oracles é um jogo indie brasileiro que vem como um roguelike diferente, no qual se usa dados em vez de cartas (como diz o nome do jogo). Há uma grande variedade de dados, que podem afetar apenas o personagem do jogador, os inimigos ou ambos, enquanto cada personagem também possui dados específicos para si.
A sua jogabilidade é um tanto simples e direta ao ponto, em que o jogador escolhe seu caminho e, nos combates, rola os dados a cada turno. Dessa forma, ele tem as habilidades que podem ser usadas naquele turno, com a possibilidade de combos, enquanto novos dados podem ser adquiridos ao longo das fases. Seus dados também podem conter riscos aos personagens, o que vem com recompensas maiores e cria uma mecânica de risco e recompensa. Além disso, há habilidades especiais que são ativadas quando a vida do personagem desce para valores específicos.
Já sua arte é bonita e chamativa, embora o excesso de azul e vermelho possa cansar ao longo do jogo. Ainda assim, é um estilo interessante e chamativo, que conversa muito bem com a história do jogo e traz todo esse ar de mundo onírico, feiticeiros astrais e uma corrupção estranha e distorcida.
Astrea: Six Sided Oracles é um jogo grátis na Epic Games ideal para fãs de roguelike, especialmente aqueles que gostam de um jogo desafiador. Não apenas isso, mas é uma boa opção para quem gosta de jogos indie, principalmente aqueles que inovam em sua jogabilidade e mecânicas.
Mechabellum
Mechabellum é um jogo de estratégia em tempo real com mechas. Entretanto, diferente do que comumente é visto no gênero, esse é um auto battler, ou seja, o jogador escolhe e posiciona suas unidades a cada rodada, nas quais elas avançam e atacam automaticamente, no formato de ondas, ou hordas. Cada unidade conta com seus pontos fortes e fracos, enquanto elas contam com vários aprimoramentos diferentes, que variam desde aumentar atributos a habilidades especiais e diferentes padrões de ataques.
Além da variedade e das fraquezas, o posicionamento das unidades também desempenha um papel importante. São elementos que transformam esse jogo em algo extremamente estratégico, enquanto mais de 20 unidades diferentes permitem uma grande variedade de combinações a cada rodada. Não apenas isso, mas há também os reforços entre as rodadas, em que o jogador pode invocar unidades especiais ou usar habilidades diferenciadas – como mísseis, fogo ou óleo no chão – o que torna cada rodada diferenciada.
O jogo tem um modo single-player, mas não é nada muito complexo. Basicamente, se resume a um modo sobrevivência e um modo de desafios. Apesar disso, esses modos podem ser jogados de forma cooperativa, com dois jogadores. Já no multiplayer, o game possui modos 1×1, 2×2 e o modo entre quatro jogadores, todos contra todos. É uma grande variedade de opções, mas o foco realmente está no multiplayer.
Mechabellum é um jogo na Epic Games para quem gosta de jogos competitivos, mas que procura fugir do tradicional. Também pode ser uma opção interessante para quem gosta de jogos de estratégia em geral, desde que não se incomode com um auto battler.
Leonardo Bueno é entusiasta de arte, literatura, games e RPG. Trabalha com tecnologia e games há mais de 10 anos.
Rachele Victoria é formada em Letras, MBA em Inovação e atua há 10 anos com comunicação e conteúdo gamer.
Amazon Prime também é feito para jogadores!
Todo mês, obtenha itens exclusivos, jogos grátis, uma assinatura gratuita na Twitch.tv e muito mais com sua assinatura Prime. Clique aqui para um teste gratuito de 30 dias.

articles.title: Axya closes $17-million Series A to modernize manufacturing procurement | BetaKit
articles.text:
Montréal-based supply chain software startup Axya has secured $17 million CAD in equity and debt Series A funding to automate procurement for manufacturers with the help of AI.
The round consisted of $12 million in equity primary capital and $5 million in venture debt from CIBC Innovation Banking. The equity portion was led by Toronto’s McRock Capital, with support from Yamaha Motor Ventures and existing backers like the Business Development Bank of Canada’s Industrial Innovation Venture Fund and Montréal’s Real Ventures.
“Manufacturers building complex products lose time and money because procurement still runs on email, spreadsheets, and ERPs that don’t talk to suppliers.”
Axya plans to use this capital to expand its platform, grow its 40-person team to 55 by the end of 2026, and deepen its presence outside of Canada.“This round is about scale,” Axya co-founder and CEO Félix Bélisle-Dockrill told BetaKit over email.
Bélisle-Dockrill said the company is deepening its AI capabilities for risk detection, optimization, and automated workflows, while growing its sales, customer success, and engineering teams. It’s also building a stronger US presence while expanding its enterprise resource planning (ERP) partnerships.
He said Axya raised money on “fundamentals, not hype,” including “strong retention, customers who expand every year, healthy margins, and a business operating close to break-even.” He noted that McRock and Yamaha deeply understand the industrial customers it serves. He did not share Axya’s Series A valuation, but claimed it was “a meaningful up round” that brings the company’s total funding to $22.4 million.
Axya was founded in 2019 by Bélisle-Dockrill, who has a background in mechanical engineering and previously worked in supplier quality for two major aerospace manufacturers. The company (formerly GRAD4) has developed an AI-powered procurement platform for large manufacturing firms. Axya’s offering integrates with manufacturers’ existing enterprise resource planning software and permits suppliers to connect via their existing channels.
“Manufacturers building complex products lose time and money because procurement still runs on email, spreadsheets, and ERPs that don’t talk to suppliers,” Bélisle-Dockrill said. “Axya plugs into the ERP they already use and applies AI to purchase orders, quotes, and supplier communication, so the same team can do more and production stays on schedule.”
Axya caters to GE Aerospace, MDA Space, and other enterprise and mid-market manufacturing customers. The company also boasts more than 80,000 suppliers in its network.
Bélisle-Dockrill claimed the startup’s annual recurring revenue (ARR) is in the “multi-million-dollar” range, noting it currently manages hundreds of millions of dollars monthly through its platform.
Axya’s Series A round comes more than four years after the company closed $5.4 million in seed funding across a $1.5-million initial round and $3.9-million extension.
McRock partner Udit Bhatnagar, who is joining Axya’s board as part of the round, said in a statement that the venture capital firm sees “an enormous market opportunity for industrial AI in the everyday work that keeps factories running,” and singled out manufacturing procurement as an area “where critical decisions still depend on scattered information.”
RELATED: Axya raises $3.9 million in seed extension to scale deployment of supply chain software
Bhatnagar told BetaKit over email that McRock was attracted to the Axya team’s understanding of the tech and this problem, and the progress it has made over the past year.
“Axya has really hit its stride over the past 12 months on two fronts,” Bhatnagar said. “First, AI has become central to what the product can do … second, that product progress is showing up commercially.”
He noted that Axya has grown capital efficiently, doubling its ARR year-over-year while posting net revenue retention near 140 percent. “That combination is what caught our attention,” he said.
Feature image courtesy Unsplash. Photo by Simon Kadula.

articles.title: EDA’s Future Is Evidence-Driven Automation
articles.text:
AI may accelerate semiconductor design, but users still need formal proof, semantic continuity, and auditable workflows to trust automation.
Key Takeaways:
AI is arriving in EDA at a time when engineers can no longer depend on brute-force scaling for performance and power improvements, and when the gaps created by disconnected point tools are becoming increasingly time-consuming to fill.
As designs expand to tens of billions of transistors and incorporate chiplets in multi-die assemblies, the hardest problems increasingly sit between tools — preserving intent, managing interdependencies, and identifying potential failures before they reach tapeout. At advanced nodes, where design costs can reach hundreds of millions of dollars and a single respin can threaten an entire program, AI’s real value will depend on whether it can accelerate various steps in the design flow while organizing and interpreting the data needed to trust the results.
The balance is between reliability and practicality. The global shortage of skilled engineers has not gone away. But it has made workflow automation more attractive, provided it can either improve the productivity of human engineers or achieve comparable results.
“Every customer is saying, ‘Give me the ability to shrink my time to results by at least 2×,’” said Ankur Gupta, executive vice president and head of EDA IC software at Siemens EDA. “Demand is pushing EDA toward a new operating model built on faster engines, smarter execution, and trusted outcomes. Acceleration may come from GPUs, machine learning, or reinforcement learning, but the larger goal is to shorten design cycles without losing confidence in the result.”
Efficiency also matters at the agent layer. Allowing any agent to call any tool may be flexible, but it can be expensive and inefficient if the underlying interfaces are poorly written. The goal is to do more of that integration work in advance so customers can either use a vendor’s agents or their own without paying unnecessary token and orchestration costs.
The economics of AI are becoming increasingly important as engineers incorporate it at various places in the design process.
“If I spend more money on tokens than a human would cost, then it doesn’t make sense,” said Thomas Andersen, vice president of the AI Excellence Group at Synopsys. “Agentic AI is useful only when it reduces the cost and complexity of production workflows. An agentic loop can perform sequences of tasks that an expert would otherwise handle manually, from automating repetitive steps to coordinating work across tools. Everybody wants to automate their workflows. They want agentic automation because that’s their way to productivity, to faster tape-out cycles, cutting costs, everything.”
The hard part isn’t dropping a tool. It’s integrating agents into real customers’ design flows.
Current challenges
Semiconductor design is inherently a multi-tool process, spanning architecture, IP configuration, integration, verification, implementation, and sign-off. The challenge is not simply moving data from one tool to another, but preserving the design intent, assumptions, and engineering context behind that data. “At the system level, where connectivity, address maps, performance constraints, and security requirements must remain consistent across many IP blocks and, increasingly, across multiple dies, engineers often serve as the integration layer,” explained Andy Nightingale, vice president of product management and marketing at Arteris.
That becomes increasingly difficult as systems grow in complexity. “The same architectural intent may be represented differently across integration, performance analysis, verification, and implementation environments,” Nightingale said. “If those representations diverge, the result can be additional verification cycles, manual rework, and late discovery of system-level issues. Better optimization between tools therefore needs to provide semantic continuity across the design flow, not simply file-format interoperability.”
Still, AI’s real impact on EDA will be less about sign-off and more about streamlining the peripheral process and data-management work around the flow. “There’s as much value there now as in the core simulators and layout tools, and that’s where AI can help you get things done much faster,” said Chris Mueth, new opportunities business manager at Keysight EDA.
Chip design is essentially a relay race involving dozens of specialized tools, including architectural exploration, RTL, lint, clock-domain crossing, formal, simulation, synthesis, place-and-route, timing and power sign-off, physical verification, equivalence checking, DFT, and post-silicon correlation.
“Each was written by a different vendor, against a different data model, with different assumptions about what ‘done’ means,” said Ashish Darbari, CEO of Axiomise. “The relay is where most of the pain lives. As the Agentic Electronic Design Automation: A Handoff Perspective survey puts it, EDA is ‘inherently multi-stage and handoff-heavy,’ and every artifact crosses tool, session, and organizational boundaries before signoff. Each transfer is a chance to lose information, silently reinterpret intent, or push a decision that was locally optimal in one tool into a globally suboptimal position downstream.”
Darbari groups the core workflow challenges into a few recurring failure modes:
That is why the next phase of AI in EDA is shifting from optimizing individual tools to coordinating the people, engines, and domain knowledge that sit between them.
Solaiman Rahim, chief product officer at ChipAgents, said tool-level AI has already improved individual engines, but the larger opportunity is coordinating the dependencies between tools and people. A DFT engineer, for example, may complete insertion correctly but still need timing analysis, expert interpretation, and another round of fixes before the work is usable. Each handoff can add days. “If you have a DFT agent handling DFT insertion and a timing agent that runs timing and debugs timing, these two agents can work together to speed up the process,” Rahim said. “Instead of taking weeks, it can take potentially just hours.”
That speedup requires more than scripts. Workflows need access to methodology, design knowledge, and context accumulated across teams. Rahim described an ontology layer that can capture why expert engineers avoid certain cells, choose particular constraints, or debug recurring failures, then make that know-how available to less experienced users and to coordinated AI workflows.
The same need for workflow-level coordination shows up outside the core digital flow, particularly where physical analysis depends on moving design data, assumptions, and results across multiple engineering domains. Satish Radhakrishnan, head of go-to-market for semiconductor and electronics at Vinci, said physics-based analysis faces the same workflow problem. Specialized tools may work well on their own, but model preparation, data movement, specialist handoffs, and result interpretation still slow the loop. By the time the analysis returns, the design may already have changed.
The problem grows as chips, packages, and systems become more tightly coupled. A chip-level change can affect package and board temperatures, mechanical stress, warpage, and reliability, none of which respects the boundary between tools or teams.
Radhakrishnan said much of the delay occurs before a solver starts. Engineers still clean geometry, create meshes, apply materials and boundary conditions, and hand results between design and simulation specialists. That process may support scheduled analysis, but it cannot provide reliable feedback each time a design changes. The goal, he said, is to move from isolated simulation checkpoints to continuous physics reasoning inside the design workflow.
Where EDA workflows are headed
ChipAgent’s Rahim predicts that the next layer of AI assistance will depend on understanding design intent, not just parsing cells and wires. “In SoC debug, for example, an AI system that understands the instruction being executed, the memory operation involved, and the relevant cycles in a waveform can help narrow a failure the way an expert designer would. The value comes from pairing intent recognition with an intelligence layer that can take action across the workflow.”
As part of this, requirements management is essential. “Today’s AI still has room for error, so you don’t let it own specifications or sign-off,” said Keysight’s Meuth. “You use it to accelerate the workflow around those decisions, not to make the decisions themselves.”
These safeguards are being implemented wherever AI is used. Paul Graykowski, director of product marketing at Cadence, pointed to one guardrail for AI-assisted testbench enhancement. Rather than allowing an agent to rewrite code unilaterally, the system surfaces the proposed refactoring for review. “The tool actually picks up those differences, and it will propose fixes,” Graykowski said. “It’s going to look at it and just say, ‘Okay, here’s the refactoring I’m proposing. Take a look at it. Do you approve?'”
That same approval model can support more autonomous regression repair, as long as the changes remain isolated until an engineer accepts them. Graykowski said one customer wanted an agent to analyze failures, make candidate fixes, rerun the regression, and return with a sandboxed result: “I’ve created a snapshot of your code, I’ve gone off, and I’ve worked on it in this sandbox. Here are the changes I’ve made. Do you approve these changes now?”
Darbari sees three emerging ways AI can reduce cross-tool friction, ranging from near-term optimization to deeper infrastructure changes. But he draws a sharp distinction between automation that preserves context and automation that simply adds another agent to the relay.
For formal verification, AI is most valuable when handoff loss is high. “LLMs can extract properties, suggest assertions, propose abstractions, and triage proofs. However, AI outputs must be independently verified, as generated assertions are hypotheses, not proof. Only a completed proof against a correct property counts as evidence. A prompt is not proof,” Darbari said.
Cadence’s Graykowski noted that kind of checked assistance could also lower the barrier to formal verification for teams without deep formal expertise. If engineers can define intent or provide a specification, an agent can help generate candidate properties and check code before it reaches simulation or a formal engine such as Jasper. The point is not to replace formal expertise, but to move more designs toward machine-checkable evidence earlier in the flow.
Further, Darbari observed that single-tool AI features are becoming table stakes. “The next competitive frontier is between tools — agentic orchestration, standardized data models, and the ability to move constraints, waivers, and evidence across tool boundaries without loss. The FluxBench evaluation of AI agents attempting end-to-end RTL-to-GDSII is a sobering reminder that the seams are still hard. The problem is not the AI. It is the lack of a shared semantic substrate for the AI to reason over.”
The need for a shared semantic substrate is where orchestration becomes more than automation. The agent has to understand not only which tool to call next, but what each result means in the larger system context.
AI can provide an intelligent orchestration layer across EDA tools. “Rather than requiring an engineer to manually inspect every result and determine the next action, an AI agent can correlate information from multiple tools, understand the wider system context, and recommend or execute the appropriate next step,” Arteris’ Nightingale said. “For example, it could identify a system-level performance issue, relate that issue to an architectural or configuration decision, make a controlled change, and rerun the relevant analysis to determine whether the result has improved.”
A fundamental shift in AI’s evolution involves moving from operating inside individual tools to operating between tools. Standardized interfaces can make EDA capabilities accessible to agents, but tool access alone is not enough.
“AI also needs domain-specific context, a consistent representation of design intent, controlled permissions, and measurable results against which its actions can be checked. In this model, AI provides reasoning and orchestration while established EDA engines continue to provide deterministic analysis and verification,” Nightingale explained.
Rahim expects compute to keep moving up the stack, first from tools to workflows, and eventually from workflows into chip-design-specific models. Today’s frontier models are not yet specialized, cost-effective, or physically aware enough to generate fully verified, PPA-optimized RTL, analog layouts, advanced packaging, or netlists on demand. But he believes that capability will improve as models absorb more workflow knowledge and domain context. “We are confident we can tackle the problem because our customers are pulling us. Semiconductors are becoming a commodity. The number of projects they have to do, the number of layouts, and the analog experts they have available no longer scale. Because of that, our customers need a solution in that space, and they are looking for a partner to work with. They are willing to share a lot of that layout knowledge for us to train on.”
Additionally, Vinci’s Radhakrishnan said that AI can remove repetitive work around physics analysis by preparing inputs, invoking the right tools, carrying results forward, and comparing alternatives within engineer-defined boundaries. But the agent is only as useful as the analysis beneath it. If simulation still requires hours of manual setup and days to run, an AI front end does not solve the bottleneck. Agentic workflows become useful when the underlying analysis is fast, automated, deterministic, and production-scale.
In Vinci’s case, the approach is to ingest native design files and pair pretrained physics models with GPU-native numerical physics kernels, producing solver-accurate results without human meshing or customer-specific training data. Radhakrishnan said the point is not probabilistic simulation-by-chatbot, but repeatable physics results that can be used while the design is still changing.
Many companies are now using agentic AI or other types of AI to enhance workflows or optimize tools in the EDA process, as well as for other reasons. Mo Faisal, founder and CEO of Movellus, sees this as an advantage for new companies. “They’re starting from scratch, and I’m a little jealous of companies born in the last month. They don’t have the baggage, at least in Silicon Valley. The most common use I’ve seen is automatic customer ticket triage, customer success, and customer support. You put in the documentation and all of your context. When a customer ticket comes in, it is automatically processed, though there’s still a human in the loop. That workflow is probably the earliest in terms of benefiting from agentic AI first.”
From a product development point of view, agentic AI is being used to create product definition specs and do quick prototyping. “Product management is blurring with engineering,” Faisal observed. “Design is product management and engineering, so the workflow changes are happening there for the open-minded teams,” Faisal noted. “In other areas like legal and accounting, etc., that’s low-hanging fruit, but bringing agentic AI into complex engineering workflow- that’s the really interesting part here. It’s definitely happening. People have libraries of skill files now, so with whatever they’re doing for their workflow, they have a bunch of skill files that are skilled in a certain step; then models are called in as they’re processing that. Yet, while this is true in Silicon Valley, if you go somewhere else, it’s not happening yet.”
Raising the abstraction
As the industry gains experience with AI, EDA workflows are likely to become increasingly intent-driven. “Rather than directly operating every tool and manually translating information between different environments, engineers will increasingly be able to specify objectives such as performance targets, connectivity requirements, security policies, or implementation constraints,” Nightingale said. “AI agents can then help determine which analyses and tools are required to meet those objectives and coordinate the necessary iterations across the design flow.”
This will make verification even more important. As agents are trusted to make larger changes and run longer workflows, every action will need an observable, verifiable outcome. “The most effective future EDA environments are therefore likely to combine AI-driven exploration and orchestration with deterministic engineering tools that continuously provide ground truth. The objective is not autonomous chip design for its own sake, but to reduce repetitive tool interactions and manual translation so engineers can spend more time making architectural and system-level decisions,” he said.
Radhakrishnan said the first challenge is to remove discrete bottlenecks, such as model preparation, analysis setup, and result comparison. Over time, those steps can become part of connected design loops in which an agent proposes a change, initiates the right physics analysis, checks the result against requirements, and either explores another option or sends the design to an engineer for review.
That would enable engineering teams to consider many more ideas. In fact, engineers who now test a handful of options may be able to examine hundreds or thousands, turning design exploration from a scheduled event into an iterative, more creative part of daily engineering work. But Radhakrishnan noted that the boundary between automation and human judgment will still matter. Early exploration may tolerate more autonomy, but validation and signoff require traceability, reproducibility, and deterministic results.
The longer-term opportunity is a design environment where AI agents coordinate specialized tools while deterministic physics keeps pace with the ideas engineers generate. In that model, physical behavior is evaluated throughout the flow, not only at scheduled checkpoints.
Axiomise’s Darbari pointed to visible shifts, each of which he expects to accelerate over the next two to three years. “The first shift is from tool-level AI to flow-level evidence. The first generation of AI in EDA sold productivity. The second will be judged on evidence. A signoff report that says, ‘The AI copilot converged the design in 40% less time,’ is interesting to a project manager. A signoff report that says ‘these properties are proven, these are bounded, these are AI-suggested and not yet checked, here is the reproducibility record,’ is what a safety, security, or automotive customer will accept. The current infatuation with autonomy will give way to an insistence on auditability. The second shift is occurring from simulation confidence to proof-backed signoff. The shift I care about most is from ‘we ran a lot of simulation, and everything looked green’ to ‘we can point at machine-checkable evidence for the properties that matter, and AI helped us get there faster.’ AI-assisted property extraction, agentic coverage closure, and LLM-driven abstraction discovery are real accelerators, but their output has to land on a formal engine that produces deterministic proof, or the confidence is theater. Apple’s Hilbert system, which wraps informal LLM reasoning around Lean 4, is the clearest public example of the architecture that will win. AI for exploration. Formal for correctness closure.”
Another wrinkle is that AI silicon splits into two verification and signoff regimes. “Training hardware lives or dies on distributed progress, collective operations, numerically valid reductions, and silent-data-corruption resilience across large clusters,” Darbari added. “Inference hardware, especially decode-heavy serving, lives on KV-cache ownership, scheduling, isolation, fairness, and tail latency. The cross-tool optimizations that matter for a training accelerator don’t matter for an inference tile. The AI-in-EDA story will fragment along the same lines. AI will not remove the need for handoffs. A boundary will always exist between architectural intent and implementation, between design and verification, and between pre-silicon proof and post-silicon behavior. AI can compress the reconciliation tax at each boundary and give engineers more time for the questions only humans can answer. Use AI for speed. Use formal for truth. Treat the boundaries between tools as places to accumulate evidence, not places to lose it.”
That shift from tool-level automation to flow-level evidence also changes what EDA companies and engineering teams have to organize around.
Organizational changes required
Tool vendors face the same organizational challenge as their customers. Agents built inside individual product groups can recreate the silos they are supposed to remove. Synopsys’ Andersen said the shift has to be guided from the top, not left entirely to bottom-up experimentation. “Every product team tends to say, ‘I’m going to build an agent in my domain, but we have to look at the whole flow.”
That matters because agentic EDA will fail if it simply adds another layer of locally optimized automation. To reduce handoff loss, organizations need shared ownership of the end-to-end flow, common data and permission models, and metrics that measure whether agents improve engineering outcomes rather than merely execute more steps.
Rahim expects workflows to advance over the next six months, especially in root-cause analysis, verification, timing closure, physical design, analog, and advanced packaging. But he cautioned that complex, fully optimized designs remain beyond current frontier models. The likely path, he said, is gradual, with specialized workflows becoming more capable, workflow knowledge moving into model layers, and chip-design models becoming more physically aware through collaboration with customers and foundries.
Graykowski succinctly framed where AI belongs in this flow: “We’re leveraging these tools as assistants, not replacements. You have to guide it. They’re the junior engineer. You’re the senior engineer.”
That may be the most practical way to think about AI’s role in EDA. It will not eliminate the boundaries between specification, implementation, verification, signoff, packaging, and post-silicon learning. Nor will it make probabilistic answers acceptable where deterministic proof is required. Its value will come from what happens at those boundaries: whether agents can carry intent, assumptions, constraints, results, and proof across the flow without losing meaning. If they can, evidence-driven automation becomes more than a productivity story. It becomes the foundation for EDA workflows that execute faster, are easier to audit, and are safer to trust.

articles.title: L’IA d’INTERPOL a passé au crible 108 000 images pour identifier 126 suspects
articles.text:
Plus de 108 000 visages extraits de la propagande djihadiste en ligne ont été triés par des agents d'intelligence artificielle, puis soumis au système de reconnaissance faciale d'INTERPOL. Au terme de l'opération Shams II, les enquêteurs ont identifié 126 combattants terroristes étrangers présumés.
Du 1er au 5 juin, INTERPOL a réuni à Tunis vingt-huit policiers et experts de onze pays, de la Côte d'Ivoire à l'Ouzbékistan en passant par l'Irak et les Philippines. Ces enquêteurs ont passé en revue les photos et vidéos publiées en ligne par des groupes djihadistes, dont ils ont extrait 108 076 images de visages. L'objectif était de retrouver des combattants terroristes étrangers. D'après le bilan de l'opération publié par INTERPOL, l'Union européenne a financé ces travaux, avec le soutien du Bureau de lutte contre le terrorisme des Nations unies. Les délégations des onze pays ont aussi rencontré des représentants de l'industrie du jeu vidéo en ligne pour évoquer la radicalisation des jeunes joueurs.
Des agents d'IA pour écarter 94 % des images
Avant toute comparaison biométrique, les 108 076 images ont été confiées à des agents d'IA programmés et à des scripts générés par IA. Ces programmes étaient chargés de supprimer les doublons et d'écarter les clichés trop flous ou mal cadrés. À l'issue de ce tri, 6 362 visages uniques et de qualité suffisante ont été conservés, soit environ 6 % du lot de départ. D'après TechRadar, les enquêteurs ont ainsi évité l'examen manuel de près de 94 % des images.
Ces 6 362 visages ont ensuite été comparés aux photos du système de reconnaissance faciale d'INTERPOL (IFRS). Cette base de données est alimentée par les photos transmises par la majorité des pays membres de l'organisation. Chaque nouveau visage y est encodé automatiquement avant d'être comparé aux modèles faciaux enregistrés. Selon INTERPOL, plusieurs milliers de personnes ont été identifiées grâce à cette base depuis sa création.
Aucune correspondance n'a toutefois été retenue sans contrôle humain. Des officiers formés à une méthode reconnue par les experts internationaux ont examiné chaque résultat, avant de lui attribuer l'un des trois verdicts prévus, du « candidat potentiel » au résultat « non concluant ». Grâce aux correspondances confirmées, les enquêteurs ont complété des dossiers de renseignement ouverts auparavant par de possibles localisations et des éléments sur l'entourage des suspects. Ces informations sont désormais versées aux bases de données d'INTERPOL. La justice de plusieurs pays de l'opération exploite ces pistes, notamment dans le dossier de deux combattants terroristes étrangers présumés, actuellement détenus.
Le silence d'INTERPOL sur l'origine de ses outils d'IA
Toujours selon son bilan, INTERPOL n'a nommé ni les modèles d'IA employés ni leurs fournisseurs. Faute de précision, TechRadar envisage que ces « scripts générés par IA » soient de simples programmes d'automatisation, écrits avec l'aide d'un grand modèle de langage, et non des systèmes conçus pour la lutte antiterroriste. Pour suivre les fonds illicites, les enquêteurs ont aussi utilisé des outils de traçage de cryptomonnaies, sans marque ni éditeur cité. Ils ont ensuite adressé trois demandes urgentes à un prestataire de services sur actifs numériques afin d'obtenir les données de certains de ses clients et d'entraver le financement du terrorisme.
María Carmen Muñoz González dirige la lutte contre le terrorisme à INTERPOL. Elle a salué dans Shams II la preuve de « la valeur d'une coopération policière internationale associée à des capacités d'analyse responsables, assistées par l'IA ». L'organisation précise que des officiers ont relu les résultats pour garantir le respect de ses règles de traitement des données.
L'encadrement de la reconnaissance faciale policière est un sujet sensible en France. En mars, nous avons relayé une enquête de Disclose sur des policiers et gendarmes qui utilisaient la reconnaissance faciale lors de contrôles d'identité, en dehors de ce que la loi autorise.
INTERPOL rappelle que plusieurs milliers d'images issues de Shams II sont encore en attente d'être traitées, et le nombre de suspects identifiés pourrait donc augmenter.

articles.title: Une station au sol de Starlink servant de relais à l'Ukraine incendiée en Pologne, la piste d'un sabotage russe évoquée
articles.text:
Un incendie a touché ce mercredi 23 septembre, vers 21 heures, une station au sol de Starlink en Pologne. La radio RMF FM a été la première à en parler. Le site se trouve à Wola Krobowska, un village situé à une quarantaine de kilomètres au sud de Varsovie.
D’après plusieurs médias polonais, dont Wirtualna Polska et Interia, le tableau électrique et le groupe électrogène de secours du site ont été endommagés. Les pompiers ont maîtrisé le feu. Des pompiers cités par RMF FM penchent pour un incendie volontaire. Le porte-parole des pompiers de Grójec, lui, a refusé de répondre sur cette piste, et un court-circuit n’est pas écarté à ce stade. Personne n’a été blessé.
L’Agence de sécurité intérieure (ABW) et le Bureau central d’enquête de la police (CBŚP) ont été alertés. L’affaire est sensible, car la Pologne, frontalière de l’Ukraine, accueille l’une des rares stations au sol de Starlink dans la région.
Comme l’indiquait le gouvernement polonais en mars 2022, Wola Krobowska et Kaunas, en Lituanie, étaient alors les deux stations terrestres desservant les utilisateurs situés en Europe centrale. Le gouvernement précisait que des satellites survolant l’Ukraine s’y connectaient également. ce qui en fait un relais pour les internautes ukrainiens. L’ouverture du service dans ce pays date de fin février 2022, deux jours après le début de l’invasion russe.
Des sites officieux comme Starlink Coverage Tracker et cette carte Google Maps personnalisée recensent aussi ces deux localités parmi les stations au sol attribuées à Starlink. Sur Reddit et X, des passionnés signalent d’autres sites près d’Istanbul (Turquie), non loin de Sofia (Bulgarie) et à l’est de l’Autriche. D’autres stations existent ailleurs en Europe, plus loin de l’Ukraine.
D’après Defence24, un média polonais spécialisé dans la défense, la station de Wola Krobowska compte une douzaine d’antennes en forme de dôme, d’environ deux mètres de diamètre. Elle est exploitée par Exatel, un opérateur télécom qui appartient à l’État polonais. Des photos du site sont disponibles en ligne, notamment sur Reddit.
Aucune coupure durable d’Internet n’a été signalée à ce stade.
Une station au sol, qu’on appelle aussi passerelle, relie les satellites au réseau Internet classique. Le signal d’un abonné part de son antenne vers un satellite, qui le renvoie vers l’une de ces stations branchées sur la fibre optique. Mais les satellites Starlink peuvent aussi s’échanger des données par laser, ce qui permet de faire passer le trafic par d’autres stations.
Starlink représente en tout cas un enjeu militaire important dans la guerre en Ukraine, car cette constellation joue un rôle central sur le front ukrainien. En début d’année, SpaceX a coupé les terminaux utilisés par l’armée russe, ce qui a ouvert la voie à une contre-attaque ukrainienne. Kiev n’entend pas non plus laisser Moscou déployer des systèmes capables de perturber le réseau, en témoigne cette attaque de drones ukrainiens contre des systèmes de brouillage russes.
Varsovie pointe déjà la Russie
Interrogé par TVN24, Krzysztof Gawkowski, vice-premier ministre et ministre du Numérique, a jugé qu’on ne peut pas exclure un sabotage. Sans attendre la fin de l’enquête, il a ensuite parlé d’un incendie criminel, qui relève selon lui du mode opératoire des services russes. Le ministre de la Justice, Waldemar Żurek, a déclaré sur la radio RMF FM, dans des propos repris par Interia, que le pays a « conscience des attaques hybrides contre la Pologne » et qu’un sabotage n’est pas exclu.
Si la piste russe se confirmait, l’incendie serait un nouvel épisode de la guerre hybride que Moscou mène en Europe pour affaiblir le soutien à l’Ukraine. On parle de guerre hybride pour des attaques menées sans déclaration de guerre, comme des sabotages ou des cyberattaques.
La Pologne a déjà accusé Moscou d’être derrière des attaques de ce genre.
En mai 2025, Donald Tusk, Premier ministre polonais, a attribué aux services russes l’incendie qui avait détruit le centre commercial Marywilska 44, à Varsovie. En novembre 2025, une explosion a endommagé la ligne ferroviaire Varsovie-Lublin, qui sert à acheminer l’aide vers l’Ukraine. Donald Tusk a ensuite annoncé devant le Parlement que deux Ukrainiens travaillant pour le renseignement russe avaient été identifiés et qu’ils avaient fui en Biélorussie.
