articles.title: Gemini can now call businesses for you so you don’t have to wait on hold
articles.text:
Google’s launching an “early experiment” feature on Pixel 11 that lets users delegate local business calls to Gemini, like making a reservation, checking if a product is in stock, or rescheduling an appointment. According to Google, you don’t even need to start the call to have Gemini handle it for you:
Gemini can now call businesses for you so you don’t have to wait on hold
Google’s AI can handle entire phone calls with businesses with a new Pixel 11 feature.
Instead of dialing yourself, just tell Gemini to call on your behalf using the Gemini app on your Pixel. Gemini will call the business, introduce itself, navigate automated phone menus, wait on hold, and handle the conversation with the person on the other end. You remain in control at all times with a live transcript view and the ability to take over the conversation at any point.
Google announced a similar “Call for me” feature last year that has its AI call local businesses to ask if they have a product you’re looking for, but it didn’t have an option for users to take over those phone calls. Meta is also working on a similar automated phone call feature for its Muse AI agent, although those calls reportedly might be made by a human behind the scenes. Google’s new AI calling feature is rolling out starting today as an “early preview” for “Gemini paid subscribers enrolled in the Phone by Google Public Beta on Pixel 11 in the US.”

articles.title: Autonomy Levels For Design Agents: L1 To L5 Explained
articles.text:
Determining what a system can decide, the scope it owns, how work is validated, when it asks for help, and who remains accountable for fallback and final signoff.
Agentic AI plays an important role in chip and system design, but not every “agentic” capability has the same degree of autonomy. In practice, autonomy is not binary. It is a progression from AI that optimizes bounded engineering tasks to systems that understand natural language, reason through design problems, and orchestrate multi-step workflows, each representing a different degree of autonomy.
That difference matters. When design teams compare autonomy, the useful question is not simply whether a system is “agentic.” It is what the system can decide, what scope it owns, how its work is validated, when it asks for help, and who remains accountable for fallback and final signoff.
This blog explains the practical progression from L1 through L5 and why a level label alone tells you very little unless it is tied to engineering scope, decision rights, validation depth, and human responsibility.
As designs grow larger, more heterogeneous, and harder to verify, engineering teams face a familiar challenge: the amount of work keeps expanding faster than the available time. More engineers and more scripts can help, but they do not fully solve the problem when design exploration, verification closure, implementation convergence, and signoff all require faster iteration across increasingly connected workflows.
This is where Cadence agentic AI strategy comes in. Cadence describes its agentic AI approach as super agents that orchestrate and implement complex, multi-step workflows while remaining grounded in Cadence’s AI-optimized, physics-based design and verification tools. That positioning is important because EDA autonomy is only useful when decisions can be checked against trusted computational models, design rules, electrical models, and engineering best practices.
The levels below are therefore not a race from “manual” to “fully automatic.” They are a way to compare how things change as AI takes on more responsibility: the scope of work, the degree of decision ownership, the validation loop, and the point at which the engineer must intervene.
Cadence Agentic AI transforms chip and system design with design agents. This changes the engineer’s role from manual task execution to outcome-driven oversight, increasing productivity and accelerating the delivery of higher-quality designs. In leading-edge deployments, autonomous workflows have reduced development cycles from weeks to days. The Cadence framework defines five increasing levels of autonomy.
These levels distinguish different types of capability, but they should not be treated as mutually exclusive product categories. A more autonomous workflow can incorporate Optimization AI, conversational capabilities, complex reasoning, and specialized agents from the levels beneath it.
Nor do higher levels make the earlier ones obsolete; higher-level agentic workflows depend on strong underlying agents, engineering engines, and optimization technologies. A workflow built from inadequate individual capabilities will not produce an adequate overall result.
At L1, AI improves a bounded engineering task without owning the broader workflow. The system can explore alternatives, learn from results, and optimize parameters to meet an objective defined by the engineer.
The differentiator is scope. AI may run extensive experiments in the background, but the engineer still owns the design intent, constraints, success criteria, and tradeoffs. Cadence Cerebrus AI Studio is a relevant example of AI-driven optimization for SoC implementation, using agentic AI workflows, advanced analytics, and optimization techniques to accelerate design closure and improve productivity.
If Level 1 is about computational heavy lifting, Level 2 is about reducing the communication barrier between human intent and machine syntax. Natural language becomes a practical interface to engineering tools and knowledge, enabling engineers to ask questions, request help, generate or debug code, and navigate tool capabilities in a conversational way. At L2, AI owns the interaction layer, not the full engineering objective; a fluent interface can make a tool easier to use without giving it independent authority over a design task.
L3 crosses an important threshold: the AI is no longer only optimizing parameters or translating natural language. It can reason through a bounded engineering problem, generate a proposed result, check that result through engineering tools or evaluators, and iterate based on feedback.
The differentiator is the reasoning-and-validation loop. A general-purpose model may produce plausible output, but EDA reasoning becomes useful when it is connected to linters checking, formal engines, simulation tools, APIs, or other evaluators that can test a result and provide feedback for the next iteration.
Here, mental models act as structured knowledge representations that capture design intent, hierarchy, relationships, specifications, and historical context. At this level, that context helps agents reason about a bounded task with more discipline than a prompt-only interaction could. The engineer still defines the problem, reviews consequential conclusions, and can redirect or reject the result. L3 gives the AI more responsibility for reasoning, but not unrestricted ownership of the design objective.
At L4, autonomy expands from a bounded reasoning task to a connected engineering workflow. Specialized agents coordinate planning, execution, validation, optimization, and iteration across multiple steps.
The differentiator is orchestration. Cadence AI Super Agents coordinate specialized agents across domains and tools. Cadence describes ChipStack, ViraStack, InnoStack, and AuraStack as applying agentic AI across front-end design and verification, analog design, digital implementation and signoff, PCB, and advanced packaging workflows. The engineer defines the goal, constraints, and acceptance criteria, while the system coordinates the path forward. What makes L4 different from L3 is not simply “more AI.” It is the coordination of multiple skills, tools, and agents toward a broader engineering outcome.
As the scope expands, governance becomes more important because one agent’s output may affect later steps in the flow. Shared design context, tool-based validation, monitoring, and exception handling help keep orchestration anchored in engineering reality.
L5 represents autonomous execution within a defined engineering scope. Cadence ChipStack AI Super Agent operates at Level 5 autonomy for complex chip design and verification workflows, while engineers can inspect, guide, and collaborate as needed.
The differentiator is dynamic execution. Rather than relying only on step-by-step prompts, the system evaluates intermediate results, determines next actions, and iterates toward closure across tasks such as specification understanding, RTL generation, verification planning, formal analysis, simulation, debug, and design convergence. Cadence has also described RTL validation workflows using Xcelium Logic Simulation and Jasper Formal Verification to accelerate validation.
This should not be read as AI replacing engineers across the entire chip-to-system lifecycle. The autonomy is bounded by workflow scope, trusted engines, validation, governance, and human oversight. Engineers remain responsible for critical decisions and final signoff.
The difference between L4 and L5 is not whether agents are present. Both levels can involve multiple agents, tool calls, reasoning, and validation.
At L4, the most important capability is orchestration: specialized agents coordinate work across a broader flow, but the workflow remains strongly shaped by the objectives, constraints, and checkpoints that engineers define.
At L5, more responsibility shifts to the system for determining the next action based on intermediate results. Autonomy is therefore deeper, but it is still not unlimited. A system may be highly autonomous in RTL validation or front-end design and verification without being autonomous across every design, system, or signoff decision.
That is why a level alone tells you almost nothing. It must be paired with the workflow boundary, the design domain, the validation mechanism, the fallback behavior, and the human decision points.
When evaluating an autonomy claim, design teams should ask:
As autonomy increases, human expertise moves to a different layer of the flow. The engineer’s role shifts from directing individual tool actions toward setting intent, supervising outcomes, managing exceptions, and approving consequential decisions. The location of human involvement changes. Accountability does not.
Fallback ownership is therefore part of the taxonomy. Engineering organizations need to understand what happens when an output fails validation, a constraint cannot be met, or the system encounters an exception. An autonomy level is credible only when the fallback path is explicit.
Autonomy in EDA should not be evaluated solely by the level label. The practical value of the L1-to-L5 taxonomy is that it gives design teams a neutral way to compare capabilities without assuming that every “agentic” system provides the same independence, engineering coverage, or governance. The best question is not “What level is it?” but “What can it decide, what can it execute, how is it validated, and where does the engineer remain accountable?”
Achieving higher autonomy requires more than adding a large language model to an EDA interface. A practical design-agent architecture typically needs several interconnected layers.
First is context: agents need access to design intent, specifications, constraints, hierarchy, tool outputs, historical experiments, and the design’s current state. In Cadence’s five levels, shared mental models help convert specifications, design sources, and historical context into a structured knowledge base that downstream agents can use.
Second is reasoning: the system must determine what action is appropriate given that context. In EDA, that reasoning must be domain-grounded because chip design decisions depend on design hierarchy, constraints, verification state, physical behavior, and tool-specific semantics.
Third is tool execution: agents need controlled access to synthesis, simulation, verification, implementation, analysis, and other engineering tools. Cadence AI Super Agents are grounded in trusted EDA engines, AI-optimized, physics-based design and verification tools.
Fourth is feedback: key actions must produce observable or measurable results—such as logs, violations, coverage signals, simulation outcomes, PPA metrics, or verification status—that can inform the next decision. Finally, orchestration coordinates specialized agents, tracks workflow state, and supports governed execution, enabling teams to monitor progress, intervene when needed, and keep autonomous activity within defined engineering boundaries.
This is why domain-specific agentic AI matters in EDA. Generic language models can produce plausible artifacts, but reliable chip design requires structured design context, tool-specific semantics, verification feedback, and trusted computational engines.

articles.title: Efficient MoE Training for Biological Foundation Models | NVIDIA Technical Blog
articles.text:
As language models grow, scaling dense architectures becomes increasingly expensive. In a dense transformer, every token passes through every layer, so adding capabilities increases computation for both training and inference.
Mixture-of-experts (MoE) architectures take a different approach to scaling by using many subnetworks, or experts, while activating only a small subset for each token.
This tradeoff has made MoE architectures increasingly attractive to the large language model (LLM) community. They can scale model capacity more efficiently, but the benefits depend heavily on implementation. Fragmented expert computation can reduce GPU utilization. Routing adds communication overhead, and larger parameter footprints create memory and distributed-training challenges. NVIDIA Transformer Engine (TE) helps address these bottlenecks with optimized primitives for grouped expert computation, kernel fusion, and low-precision training. As biological foundation models grow in parameter count and sequence length, these primitives can improve GPU efficiency while expanding model capacity.
This tutorial shows how to put these techniques into practice with the NVIDIA BioNeMo MoE recipe and TE. You’ll see how GroupedLinear improves expert computation, MXFP8 reduces memory use, and the GroupedMLP kernel fuses quantization, SwiGLU, and routing-weight scaling. Together, these capabilities provide a practical reference for efficiently training MoE-based biological foundation models.
Prerequisites
Before you begin, you need:
- Familiarity with Python, PyTorch, and distributed training concepts
- An NVIDIA CUDA-enabled environment—you can use the linked Dockerfile or install the recipe requirements
- At least two GPUs for expert parallelism; NVIDIA Blackwell GPUs are required to use the fused MXFP8 GroupedMLP kernel
Challenge 1: Fragmented expert kernels
MoE models replace a single dense feed-forward block with multiple expert networks. A naive implementation, however, can trigger excessive kernel launches. For example, the Hugging Face baseline implementation iterates over all experts in a Python loop, with each expert triggering separate kernel launches.
for expert_idx, expert_layer in enumerate(self.experts):
    idx, top_x = torch.where(expert_mask[expert_idx])
    current_state = hidden_states[None, top_x].reshape(-1, hidden_dim)
    current_hidden = expert_layer(current_state) * routing_weights[top_x, idx, None]
    final_hidden_states.index_add_(0, top_x, current_hidden)
Grouped execution preserves the individual expert matrices but submits their work together. TE’s GroupedLinear applies multiple linear transformations in one call by gathering the expert weights and input tokens. Because each expert can receive a different number of tokens, GroupedLinear accepts per-expert token counts (split_sizes). It submits the local experts through the TE grouped GEMM path instead of launching one PyTorch Linear operation per expert, reducing launch and scheduling overhead.
Use GroupedLinear as follows. Each expert retains its own weight tensor (weight0, weight1, and so on), and the call accepts the per-expert token counts as an additional positional argument:
from transformer_engine.pytorch.ops import GroupedLinear
experts_gate_up = GroupedLinear(
    num_groups=num_local_experts,
    in_features=hidden_size,
    out_features=2 * intermediate_size,
    bias=False,
    dtype=torch.bfloat16,
    device="cuda",
)
gate_up_output = experts_gate_up(tokens, split_sizes)
Compared with the Python loop, this approach submits the gate-up projections as one grouped operation instead of multiple separate calls.
Hugging Face Transformers also provides grouped_mm. However, TE can fuse GroupedLinear with MXFP8 quantization, activation, routing-weight scaling, and intermediate data movement into a GroupedMLP kernel, as shown in the later sections.
Challenge 2: Large model size and activation memory
MoE architectures increase total parameter capacity, and genomics workloads often use long sequences, which puts pressure on activation memory during training. BF16 uses 16 bits to represent each model weight and activation.
The BioNeMo recipe uses TE to support FP8 and MXFP8 training, reducing memory use. Both formats represent weight and activation values with 8 bits instead of 16. The main difference between FP8 and MXFP8 is scaling granularity: MXFP8 assigns a scaling factor to each block of 32 consecutive values, helping preserve numerical range and accuracy. On NVIDIA Blackwell GPUs, MXFP8 is hardware-accelerated, enabling MXFP8 GEMMs to use specialized Tensor Core instructions. For details about MXFP8 and block scaling, see the Transformer Engine FP8 primer.
Challenge 3: Quantization overhead in low-precision training
Although most training computation uses 8-bit precision, the model retains its master weights in 16 bits. The training framework therefore adds quantization and dequantization steps to convert between formats. Quantization converts BF16 weights and activations to MXFP8 before the low-precision GEMM; dequantization converts the result back to the higher-precision format. A naive path performs these steps as separate operations, motivating the fused MLP path described next.
fp8_recipe = te_recipe.MXFP8BlockScaling()
model = TEMixtralMXFP8ForCausalLM(config, fp8_recipe=fp8_recipe, dispatcher=dispatcher)
The TE autocast API enables MXFP8 precision for the model’s forward and backward passes:
with te.autocast(enabled=True, recipe=self._fp8_recipe):
    for decoder_layer in self.layers:
        hidden_states = decoder_layer(hidden_states)
See the BioNeMo recipe for the complete code.
To use the fused MLP, import the Transformer Engine Sequential API to chain together gate_up, ScaledSwiGLU, and down. The API also folds dequantization into the fused path. ScaledSwiGLU combines the routing probabilities (“scales”) with the expert feed-forward network computations.
from transformer_engine.pytorch.ops import GroupedLinear, ScaledSwiGLU, Sequential
experts_ffn = Sequential(GroupedLinear(gate_up), ScaledSwiGLU(), GroupedLinear(down))
The TE Sequential API scans the operations and, when the pattern matches, replaces the GroupedLinear → ScaledSwiGLU → GroupedLinear sequence with a fused operation object: ForwardGroupedMLP_CuTeGEMMSwiGLU_MXFP8 for the forward pass and a matching fused backward operation. This reduces framework overhead, fuses the SwiGLU and probability-scaling work into the grouped MLP path, and avoids materializing some intermediate results.
Results
These are several of the optimizations in the BioNeMo recipe. In our training benchmark on eight NVIDIA B200 Tensor Core GPUs, the recipe delivered up to 2.21x the throughput of the Hugging Face baseline.
Run the recipe
Start with the two-GPU L0_sanity configuration to confirm that expert parallelism and the training environment work correctly:
torchrun --nproc_per_node=2 train_fsdp2_ep.py --config-name L0_sanity
After validation, scale to the Mixtral-8x7B configuration with expert parallelism (EP=8) and MXFP8 precision across eight GPUs:
torchrun --nproc_per_node=8 train_fsdp2_ep.py --config-name L1_8x7B_ep checkpoint.ckpt_dir=/path/to/ckpt
Select BF16 or MXFP8 based on your GPU and memory requirements and set the data-parallel and expert-parallel sizes so their product equals the total GPU count. The recipe README includes launch, checkpoint, and benchmark commands.
Try the Mixtral Native Transformer Engine recipe in BioNeMo Recipes and learn more about the optimized MoE kernels in the NVIDIA Transformer Engine documentation.

articles.title: The $6.8M credit engine hidden inside a Nigerian cassava patch | TechCabal
articles.text:
When Alexander Zanders stood on a patch of land in Oyo State in 2015, he planned to build a simple processing plant. But as the naira plunged, importing machinery became impossible. Forced to pivot, Zanders bought 100 acres, started farming himself, and ran a small experiment supplying 15 local maize growers with inputs on credit. The result? Crop yields tripled, farmer revenues doubled, and Zanders extracted the financial signals hidden in the soil. In this feature, OPEYEMI KARREM tells the story of how UfarmX has facilitated over $6.8 million in trade across 10,000+ farmers in Nigeria, Senegal, and Liberia—not by farming or direct lending, but by turning rural farm data into credit ratings for commercial banks and retailers.
In 2015, Alexander Zanders stood on 2,000 acres of land in Oyo State, southwestern Nigeria, recently gifted to him by his grandmother. The land coincided with Zanders’ burgeoning interest in agriculture, and as he began considering how to commercialise it, he noticed streaks of white powder lining the roadsides surrounding the property. It was cassava. Local farmers were harvesting the crop, processing it, and sun-drying it before turning it into garri—a dietary staple across Nigeria. An entrepreneur at heart, Zanders immediately spotted a supply chain he could plug into.
“My initial goal was simply to build a cassava processing plant because I figured that the local population would feed the plant, and I’d be able to make money from there,” Zanders told TechCabal in an interview in August.
Zanders had not originally come to Nigeria to farm. He founded his first company in 2011 while still an undergraduate, capitalising on supply-chain disruptions following the Japanese tsunami. He bootstrapped an export business that generated over $15 million in sales across Nigeria, Dubai, and the Caribbean. A subsequent venture into real estate, however, failed miserably.
Agriculture became a serious pursuit after the birth of his daughter in 2015. While living in the United States, a friend whose family worked in agribusiness invited him to the Sunbelt Ag Expo in Moultrie, Georgia. The event offered Zanders his first real sense of the scale of industrial food production, convincing him of the commercial potential within the sector.
The Georgia trip, combined with his grandmother’s gift of land, converted that interest into an actionable strategy, while the cassava drying along the roads provided a concrete business model. Yet the processing plant was never built.
As Zanders finalised his business plan and paperwork, Nigeria’s macroeconomic environment worsened. The Central Bank of Nigeria had pegged the official exchange rate at roughly ₦197 ($0.15) to the dollar, but by June 2016, the naira had plummeted to ₦283 ($0.21) per dollar, closing the year at approximately ₦305 ($0.23). The sudden devaluation drastically altered the economics of importing heavy machinery for the processing facility.
“I was looking to secure some funding from a bank to be able to get the equipment for the cassava processing plant,” Zanders said. “But since the Naira was in a downward spiral, I ended up taking what I thought was just going to be one year to travel across the continent, attend different conferences, and learn more about agriculture and our needs for value addition on the continent of Africa.”
That single year stretched into three. In 2019, he incorporated UfarmX as a credit infrastructure business designed to evaluate farmer creditworthiness using proprietary data, allowing agro-retailers to extend inputs on credit. However, before UfarmX became a fintech infrastructure platform, it operated as a working farm.
The farm as a laboratory
When the COVID-19 lockdown halted global travel in 2020, Zanders revisited his agricultural plans. The initial concept for UfarmX centred on connecting the African diaspora with local farmland. With international travel ground to a halt, he pivoted toward a more direct hands-on project.
However, a family dispute over the 2,000 acres gifted by his grandmother forced a strategic detour. Zanders instead acquired 100 acres independently, spending the next year securing title documentation before planting cassava, maize, and soybeans in 2021.
“Our production level was significantly higher than the other farmers in the local area,” Zanders said. “I’m not a farmer by profession. So, at a surface level, it just looked like we were all farming on the same land. I didn’t really understand why.”
Instead of chalking it up to better farming practices, Zanders began speaking with farmers around him and noticed that the difference was in what the farmers could afford to put into their land.
“These farmers just simply didn’t have the same access to quality, drought-resistant seeds and fertilisers that we did on our farm,” he said.
Rather than attributing the gap to superior technique, Zanders interviewed local growers and realised the true differentiator lay in capital: local farmers simply could not afford quality inputs.
“At the end of that first pilot, what we saw in terms of results was that farmers’ yields not only tripled, but their revenues also more than doubled,” Zanders said. “And we were still able to make a significant profit ourselves off of the margins on the inputs to the credit facilities.”
UfarmX also secured off-take agreements and purchase orders prior to harvest, guaranteeing farmers a direct market. The pilot established a viable business model: earning revenue by facilitating agricultural trade while derisking farm operations.
“As we continued supporting these farmers, we started noticing constant themes in the datasets themselves that differentiated the farmers that were able to successfully repay us versus not,” Zanders said. “We felt that we had essentially identified the data within the data itself.” That data became the foundation of UfarmX’s credit underwriting model.
How the UfarmX credit engine works
Farmers onboard onto UfarmX through three channels: agro-retail partners, community agents, or contracted farmer cooperatives. At the retail level, store owners act as distribution partners, introducing smallholders to input financing at the point of sale.
Regardless of the onboarding channel, underwriting takes place exclusively on UfarmX’s infrastructure. The system ingests farmer data, processes it through proprietary algorithms, and generates an automated credit decision. While Zanders declined to reveal the full scoring algorithm, he confirmed that the model evaluates full Know-Your-Customer (KYC) records alongside geospatial and socioeconomic metrics, including plot proximity to major roads and markets, crop type, projected yield, farming tenure, and household size.
A farmer who is approved for the credit facility pays a transaction fee upfront, receives agricultural inputs on credit, and repays according to their creditworthiness. Farmers in the highest credit tier can repay after harvest, while those in lower tiers make monthly payments, according to Zanders.
UfarmX said it guarantees every farmer it approves to its retail partners, meaning that it pays the retailer if an approved farmer fails to repay. An insurance partner covers 80% of that risk, Zanders said. UfarmX generates revenue from transaction fees, interest spreads, and software-as-a-service (SaaS) fees paid by businesses using its technology.
The model is operating in a market where several companies are trying to solve the same financing problem, including Kenya’s Apollo Agriculture, Nigeria’s ThriveAgric, and Babban Gona.
“We don’t look to compete with banks and retailers; we’re not even really competing with other ag tech companies,” Zanders said. “We feel that our success bolsters the entire ecosystem and enables all the players within the ecosystem to successfully extend credit with minimal risk.”
The company said its cumulative default rate across its direct-lending and retail networks is 9.03%. On the retail model, however, the net default rate falls to 1.17% after insurance. UfarmX says it has facilitated more than $6.8 million in agricultural commerce, working with more than 10,000 farmers and over 70 vetted retail partners across Nigeria, Senegal, and Liberia.
Zanders noted that the company plans to launch a credit-scoring Application Programming Interface (API) that will allow banks, financial institutions, development finance institutions, and other lenders to plug directly into its underwriting infrastructure.
UfarmX also plans to expand into Kenya, its first East African market, by the end of 2026. The company said the expansion will be part of its effort to test the underwriting model in another agricultural and financial market.
Having started on a 100-acre farm in Oyo State, UfarmX is now building the financial infrastructure for an entire continent. “UfarmX is no longer in the business of direct lending,” Zanders concluded. “We are an enabler. We are building critical rails for African agriculture.”
True scale demands moving beyond surface-level integrations to robust execution. We’ve filtered the noise out of Moonshot 2026, optimising the conference strictly for high-calibre connections between startup founders, global financial operators, enterprise leaders and individuals rewiring Africa’s technical frameworks. articles.title: Oi está com a conta quase zerada e sem condições de pagar ex-funcionários • Tecnoblog
articles.text:
Oi está com a conta quase zerada e sem condições de pagar ex-funcionários
Cerca de mil ex-trabalhadores aguardam pagamentos de verbas rescisórias. Valores somam R$ 72 milhões.
A Oi informou à Justiça que ficou com apenas R$ 10 mil em caixa em setembro e não tem condições financeiras de cumprir o acordo para pagar as verbas rescisórias dos quase mil trabalhadores demitidos. Os valores devidos são estimados em R$ 72 milhões.
A situação ocorre após a Justiça do Rio de Janeiro decretar novamente a sua falência. Segundo informações do site Convergência Digital, os salários dos funcionários que permanecem contratados estão em dia, mas não há previsão para o pagamento das rescisões.
A Oi não apresentou uma data, mas propôs à Justiça que os ex-funcionários recebam por rateios conforme a disponibilidade de caixa. Caso o dinheiro não seja suficiente para quitar as verbas, o saldo seria incluído nos rateios seguintes, até o pagamento integral.
Dos R$ 72 milhões estimados, R$ 30,4 milhões correspondem às verbas rescisórias ordinárias, como saldo de salário, aviso prévio e férias proporcionais. Outros R$ 41,6 milhões são referentes à multa do FGTS. Quase R$ 12 milhões deveriam ser pagos em setembro como primeira parcela das verbas e multa do fundo.
O acordo homologado antes da falência estabelecia condições diferentes. A multa de 40% do FGTS seria quitada integralmente entre 30 e 120 dias após o desligamento, conforme a faixa salarial. As demais verbas seriam divididas em seis parcelas para funcionários com salário bruto de até R$ 5 mil e em dez parcelas para os demais, com a primeira vencendo 30 dias após a demissão.
O acerto também previa a manutenção do plano médico e hospitalar por 90 dias após a rescisão, incluindo dependentes cadastrados. A companhia ainda se comprometeu a não descontar o saldo do tíquete refeição ou alimentação creditado no mês do desligamento.
Segundo a Oi, enquanto não ocorrer a venda da Oi Soluções, divisão corporativa da operadora focada no mercado B2B (empresas e grandes clientes do governo), as obrigações precisam ser ajustadas ao fluxo de caixa disponível.
A companhia argumenta que a medida é necessária para manter provisoriamente os negócios e a prestação de serviços essenciais. O processo de alienação de ativos, porém, enfrenta outros obstáculos. Uma decisão recente da Justiça estabeleceu novas condições envolvendo bens da companhia, em mais um desdobramento do processo de falência.
A administração judicial reconheceu a relevância do pagamento das verbas trabalhistas e afirmou que, quando o acordo foi celebrado, havia perspectiva de que os valores pudessem ser pagos nos termos estabelecidos. Com a decretação da falência, porém, os pagamentos passaram a ficar sujeitos às regras do processo.
A decisão sobre a proposta apresentada pela Oi caberá à juíza Simone Gastesi Chevrand, da 7ª Vara Empresarial do Rio de Janeiro.
Este texto originalmente dizia que a Oi tinha apenas R$ 0,01 em caixa. No entanto, descobriu-se posteriormente que a rubrica na prestação de contas equivaleria a R$ 10 mil. A matéria foi corrigida.

articles.title: The Xbox reset gets ugly
articles.text:
It feels like Xbox has been in a permanent state of turmoil for at least two years now, and this week is no different. Microsoft cut 268 jobs across its gaming division this week, shuffled major studios and franchises around, and continued its Xbox “reset.”
The Xbox reset gets ugly
Another round of cuts leaves big questions over the future of Game Pass and the Xbox platform.
Layoffs have become a way of life for Xbox employees, after Microsoft started cutting thousands in early 2024 and hasn’t slowed down. The turmoil was particularly apparent when Microsoft started shutting down game studios, and the painful layoffs have had a lasting impact on morale, according to current and former Xbox employees I’ve been speaking to this week.
At the same time, Xbox hardware is under pressure, Game Pass keeps being reshaped, and the future of Xbox as a brand feels more uncertain than ever before. This week was also a reminder that Microsoft is still very much in the middle of figuring out Xbox’s future.
Nothing demonstrates the scale of change going on inside the Xbox organization than Halo. “If we lose our way with Halo, we lose our way with Xbox,” said former Xbox chief Phil Spencer in 2011. It’s been clear for years that Microsoft has lost its way with Halo, and the company has definitely lost its way with Xbox.
Instead of moving the Halo Studios team under Activision directly, Microsoft is laying off most of the studio after years of layoffs, leadership changes, and technical shifts. A shell of the team is being kept in place to handle existing games like Halo Infinite and the recently shipped Halo: Campaign Evolved. One source tells me that the next Halo game under Halo Studios was years away from shipping, so Microsoft pulled the plug instead.
I understand that some Halo Studios employees had to wait hours to find out if they had been impacted by the layoffs earlier this week. The first communication came in a public Xbox blog, before notifications were sent to employees throughout the morning.
For some, the layoffs were a relief. “I’m a jumble of thoughts and emotions, but mostly relief,” wrote former Halo Studios employee Ron B on LinkedIn. “I was miserable for the last year and a half and it’ll be nice to feel something different.”
For many others, the announcement was met with anger or confusion. “Promoted and laid off in the same week is pretty wild,” said Josh Daniels, former cinematic director at Halo Studios. Shannon Loftis, who spent nearly 30 years at Microsoft working on franchises like Fable and Project Gotham Racing, didn’t hold back on criticism of Xbox chief Asha Sharma. “Super funny that Asha Sharma said ‘clarity is kindness’ to the WSJ last week then did a half layoff today,” said Loftis in a post on Threads. “I guess Damocles’ Sword is a form of clarity, what do I know?”
Loftis was the former head of World’s Edge before she retired from Microsoft in 2022, the studio behind Age of Empires. The fan-focused studio is now being moved into Activision, with some layoffs impacting the team as part of this ongoing Xbox “reset.” Rare, the developers of Sea of Thieves, are also part of this latest shake-up, moving under Activision control. Forza developers Turn 10 Studios and Playground Games are also merging into a single studio, a year after Microsoft gutted Turn 10.
Even Obsidian is being moved out from Xbox Game Studios and under Bethesda Game Studios, where it will work on a new entry in the Fallout franchise.
Beyond the studio changes, there are also cuts to the core business planning and management areas of Xbox. “These aren’t cuts a serious business makes, in my opinion,” says video game industry analyst Mat Piscatella. Loftis was even more critical, saying “Xbox has become a business best described as ‘squandered.’ They’re [sic] squandered everything: talent, IP, time, money, gamers, community, goodwill, brand equity, stable services, profitable, knowledge.”
The changes are part of Sharma’s “most significant restructure in Xbox history.” She previously told employees that she will make significant cuts to reset the Xbox content portfolio, platform, and operations. Some of the cuts feel like they could be part of a broader restructure designed to make Xbox easier to spin off, or to operate as a wholly owned subsidiary in the same way Microsoft already does with Activision and LinkedIn. Management layers are being reduced, smaller studios are being offloaded, and the focus appears to be on larger franchises and a nearly impossible goal of reaching “more than a billion people each day.”
Beneath all the buzzwords in corporate memos, it’s clear that by moving these studios and franchises around, Sharma wants to get bigger games out quicker and at less cost. Microsoft has spent more than a decade acquiring and investing in studios under its Xbox Game Studios umbrella. At one point it had 15 dedicated first-party studios, but that part of the overall Xbox studios organization looks barren now. There’s a shell of Halo Studios for now, a team for Microsoft Flight Simulator, and the Xbox publishing arm, but beyond that all that’s really left is Forza Horizon developers Playground Games, Gears of War developers The Coalition, and inXile who are currently working on Clockwork Revolution. Sharma already has Minecraft developer Mojang reporting to her directly, and the rest have been shifted to Activision to presumably focus on multi-platform games.
Some employees I’ve been speaking to think it’s inevitable that The Coalition and inXile will be impacted by layoffs once Gears of War: E-Day and Clockwork Revolution have shipped. In fact, Microsoft already started some Coalition layoffs this week. Both studios also happen to be the ones shipping Xbox-exclusive games.
If Microsoft does continue gutting Xbox Game Studios then this also speaks volumes about the platform strategy. Many of Microsoft’s core first-party Xbox studios were established to showcase Xbox hardware. The Coalition has pushed the limits of what’s possible on Xbox consoles over the years, with real expertise on Unreal Engine that has benefited other projects at Xbox.
These studios have also contributed heavily to Xbox Game Pass. Microsoft has been tweaking its subscription service nonstop over the past couple of years, adding and removing Call of Duty from the service, flip-flopping on pricing, and making U-turns on cloud access. It’s clear that Game Pass isn’t quite working for Microsoft, despite previous promises that the service was profitable.
I’ve heard from multiple sources over the years that there has always been a tension between Xbox leadership and studios over putting games on Xbox Game Pass. Putting a title on Game Pass cannibalizes traditional buy-to-play game sales, and the return isn’t always quantified in a boost in subscription numbers. Xbox lost $300 million in Call of Duty sales because of its addition to Game Pass, prompting Microsoft to quickly reverse course on bringing new entries in the franchise to the service.
With fewer first-party studios making day-one games for Game Pass, it seems inevitable that Microsoft will tweak the Game Pass formula again. Rumors suggest that Microsoft is working on an overhaul to Game Pass that will create tiers with or without ads, much like Netflix and other streaming services. These new tiers will reportedly debut without access to day-one games, as well as add-on bundles for cloud gaming and a new family plan option. Microsoft has already pulled day-one games for its Game Pass Premium subscription, so I wouldn’t be surprised to see more changes ahead.
Significant changes to Game Pass could also reflect the reality of the Xbox hardware situation. Sources at Xbox tell me that Grand Theft Auto VI preorders are heavily skewed toward PS5, ringing yet more alarm bells about the platform. Xbox hardware revenue has now declined for three straight years, and RAMageddon is pushing the prices of Xbox Series X consoles higher and higher. It’s getting increasingly harder to predict what this all means for Project Helix, Microsoft’s next-generation Xbox console.
As you can probably tell, piecing together Microsoft’s Xbox strategy is challenging. One thing is clear, though: The cuts aren’t over yet. Microsoft says it’s roughly three-quarters of the way through its Xbox restructuring, leaving employees with the prospect of more upheaval hanging over them for the foreseeable future.

articles.title: 3D Chips Push EDA Into New Territory
articles.text:
As AI chips move to stacked, chiplet-based architectures, EDA vendors are reworking mature tools for cross-domain analysis, faster exploration, and agentic AI assistance.
Key Takeaways:
As demand for AI power and performance grows, chip designs increasingly involve 3D stacking, chiplets, and heterogeneous integration within a single package.
In a virtuous cycle, EDA tool vendors are leveraging advanced chips to simulate multi-physics challenges in a single tool instead of running individual solvers. Agentic AI is adding another layer of analysis to enable faster design exploration and automate various tasks. However, a few speed bumps remain due to the rapid progression of chip technology.
One challenge is that HPC/AI chip design must be considered across compute, memory, interconnect, power, and thermal constraints. “Today, nearly every AI accelerator has a process threshold where the hardest problems no longer live inside the chip. They live at the system boundaries,” said Artour Levin, vice president of AI silicon engineering at Microsoft.[1] “A standalone chip is not very beneficial for AI because very few things can be run on a single chip. You really need to look at the system level, and if you look at the history of EDA tools when they started, 30 or 40 years ago, it’s natural that EDA tools were designed to design chips, not a system.”
The chip-to-system threshold is where customers are facing challenges. “The design toolchain grew up around clean abstraction boundaries — cell, block, chip — with physics handled as episodic, domain-by-domain validation at the end,” said Hardik Kabaria, CEO and co-founder of Vinci. “That operating model worked when the hardest problems stayed inside those boundaries. It breaks when heat, stress, and electrical behavior move across the entire physical stack, because the physics insight arrives after the decisions that needed it have already been made. Hardware teams don’t need physics after the design is done changing. They need physics while the design is still moving.”
That requires new approaches, not a faster version of the old workflow. “It’s deterministic, solver-accurate physics that’s continuously available across chip, package, board, and system — treating physics as infrastructure rather than a late-stage checkpoint,” said Kabaria. “In hardware, plausible isn’t enough. Outputs have to be measurable, deterministic, and accurate enough to support real design decisions, which is why solver-grounded results and run-to-run reproducibility matter as much as speed.”
The central question is whether to augment existing EDA tools that have been fine-tuned and proven over many years, or create new tools because AI/HPC chip designs are so different from the monolithic chips of days gone by.
“There are decades of embedded knowledge for good reason, and a lot of long-held beliefs that work in single isolation, but maybe not when you go cross-domain,” said Henry Sheng, executive director of R&D at Synopsys.[2] “This has to be reflected within the tooling itself. How do you manage not to try to boil the ocean? If you try to reinvent everything, you won’t do it. You have to reinvent how you put things together to maintain coherency, so you don’t have different data representations and terminologies for the same thing across domains. Then, how do you bring all that into a cohesive tool?”
Heterogeneity puts more pressure on floor-planning challenges, in particular. “It becomes much harder, and that’s one of the conversations that people are having,” said Nilesh Kamdar, general manager of Keysight EDA. “Can we do the floor planning upfront? Can we make sure we all agree that this is the budget that you get for loss here, and this is the budget I get for signal path, and this is the way we are going to supply power to this complex 3D environment? That conversation starts happening up front, and it leaves very little room for negotiation later.” And while the big money says to use 3D design for AI chips, it can be applicable anywhere, Kamdar added.
Maybe in the future, 3D and heterogeneous design will be out of the box, but that’s not the reality now. “Because the manufacturing and packaging technology is evolving fast, there’s still different solutions out there,” said Michal Siwinski, executive vice president, chief product and marketing officer at Arteris. “You can do it this way. You can do it that way. It’s not yet one size fits all. Because of that, people want some differentiation. But is the technology 80% there? Is it 90% there, where anybody who actually wants to do it can do it? Yeah, I think so.”
Specific customer challenges
Customers designing 3D-ICs and multi-die assemblies for AI/HPC chips are using existing EDA tools, but they want improvements in some areas.
One challenge is interoperability across established vendors and startups. “If you want to put out compelling products in the industry, EDA tools should be very interoperable,” said Lalitha Immaneni, vice president of semiconductor R&D for advanced packaging technology and manufacturing at Intel. [3]. “I happened to look at a design last week. Just by experience, I said, ‘I don’t see enough density in some of these layers. Copper density is critical for warpage.’ I was very concerned that this might be a technical glitch. I reached out to my mechanical analysis person. I said, ‘Here you go. I think it is one of the other industry formats, but it doesn’t matter. We need to let the design team know that they might have to co-optimize the design, so they don’t get into issues later.’ It took 10 days for the analysis and a response. People looked at the design. They saw it wasn’t complete. It didn’t have some properties. Maybe it wasn’t completely routed. Then I pulled in a design engineer. They finished up with AI. They wrote some scripts, routed it, but then the extraction didn’t happen in a very prominent industry analysis capability. What I got was three pictures. One is yellow. One is red, and who knows what the other color is. And if I am a customer, as a design person, I look at it and don’t know what I need to do to the design. It makes no sense. Then I’ve got to bring 10 PhDs in a room [to fix it].”
Fig. 1: Intel’s Immaneni details the impact of complexity in AI chips. Source: Intel/DAC
Interoperable tools make it easier for customers to bring findings together. “Each of the customers should be able to pick and choose the best in class from each vendor, whether it’s mechanical analysis, design enabling, connectivity checkers, whatever it is. And all these EDA tools should agree to a CAD-neutral format, so the extractions don’t become this complex,” Immaneni noted.
For now, HPC customers are doing the best they can. “We have been living in pain for probably the last five or six years,” said AJ Tufano, distinguished engineer at Broadcom.[2] “We’re getting by, we’re surviving, we’re producing chips, but we can do a lot better.”
In the custom accelerator space, every six months — and in some cases every three months — fundamental architectural changes are happening. “The challenge that we’re faced with is how to match the pace of software, and how to do that while complexity keeps increasing. 3.5D is a large part of that,” Tufano observed.
Fig. 2: Challenges in 3D-IC and heterogeneous design. Source: Broadcom/DAC
There are wins with the challenges. “I will pause and give kudos to the folks creating these tools because it does really impress me that for the scale of the design we have, we can get this thing to run in its entirety at the level of detail that is needed,” said Tufano. “That’s phenomenal. If I look at the number of orders of [magnitude] at any given point in time to do one chip, it’s like a brownout of the lab. The compute resource there is pretty stagnant, so we’re left with a dichotomy of early analysis flows to catch gross issues, which are important, then full-blown IR signoff, which happens much too late. There’s a gap of issues that could potentially be solved in between.”
Others point to similar challenges. [3] “We are surviving right now,” said Venu Sanaka, senior director of engineering at Qualcomm. “The thermal and IR analysis are much more advanced than the other stages of analysis in terms of the multi-physics. The challenges right now are more on the exploration front. Exploration is pretty manual. I can venture out to say, where do you put the bump locations and TSVs (through-silicon vias) and thermal? Those trade-offs aren’t fast enough for our analysis in a normal design cycle. Say it’s one year or so. For this kind of partitioning analysis, we need to start much earlier, maybe three to six months. For that, you don’t have designs ready to run through all the detailed analysis, so you need an early trade-off mechanism.”
Die-to-die PPA optimizations are also tricky. “We wanted to move one block from one die to the other die in a different technology,” said Sanaka. “The power and placement implications of that are all manual right now. We don’t have any quick way of analyzing it, so we floorplan it in 2D, then we put it together and analyze it.”
Multi-chip compounds the challenge. “When I say one chip, I mean when you put in the physical index directory it is related to one chip,” said Sanaka. “Now you have multiple chips trying to come together with different technologies. The data management aspect itself is a little more challenging, and we have a lot of partners within our teams that we need to exchange data with. How do you exchange that data? These are all in the recent stages.”
Fig. 3: EDA tool solutions needed by companies designing AI chips. Source: Qualcomm/DAC
The opportunity to improve tools is large, even if there are pain points right now. “It’s clear that there’s sub-optimality,” Sheng observed. “These chips are phenomenally successful, so it’s okay for now. To fully appreciate the transformation, we’re going from fully manual to automation. We’re going from many single-domain problems to cross-domain problems. In many cases, manual design is experience-driven.”
EDA tools have undoubtedly made incremental improvements, noted Sheng. “But transformational readiness goes through everything.”
Agentic AI as an additional layer on existing tools
EDA vendors have two paths to meet HPC customers’ needs  — augment existing tools or start over. Agentic AI is making both paths possible.
“Three or four years ago, when we saw the technology starting to take off, we had this discussion,” said Vinay Patwardhan, product management group director at Cadence. [3] “When we went to customers, one piece of feedback we received was, ‘We have a hundred 2D designers. We don’t have any 3D designers, so whatever you build, make sure those hundred people can adapt your existing technology.”
Another problem concerned taping out the chip. “We say, ‘It’s a new technology. We just wrote it.’ And the customer would respond, ‘Can you build on something that is trusted so we don’t have to go through this palm tree validation loop again?’ So we made a conscious decision to say that we have our industry-standard tools. The foundries are qualified with extensive certification flows,” Patwardhan explained. “It makes sense to build on that, make it three-dimension aware, use some optimizations to do full 3D or stacking, then see how the industry is moving. When an inflection point comes, we either redevelop the whole flow, or we use some of the new techniques. That’s where we are now with the agentic flow that has come to the top. The exploration capabilities are tremendously improved, and will be tremendously improved because there are a lot of variables.”
Fig. 4: Synopsys’ Sheng and Cadence’s Patwardhan debate the readiness of EDA tools for 3D design at the Design Automation Conference. Source: Semiconductor Engineering [3]
Others agree that agents offer the extra layer needed. “AI is increasingly being used to explore configurations and identify optimal tradeoffs much faster than traditional flows, accelerating design-space exploration, especially for 2.5D and 3D-ICs, where complexity grows significantly,” noted Insaf Meliane, director of product management and marketing, at Arteris. “But AI-generated design decisions must be explainable, traceable, and validated against deterministic EDA engines and established verification methodologies before signoff.”
The latest tools already help with some of the upfront floor-planning analysis for 3D-ICs, and the agentic layer with natural language prompts can be turned on or off to save token use.
“At a very abstract level, we can look at boxes in different colors and with a few clicks, you can change the materials or properties,” said Keysight’s Kamdar. “You can choose to have a very deep via layer, and you can see what the impact would be on your electrical performance. Or you can have a very thin via layer. It’s a choice of, ‘What if?’ This is not a deep optimization problem. This is an architectural problem. The architecture of these designs has some boundary conditions. You can’t just shoot for the moon. Largely, it’s the materials that people are operating in. The size constraint is fixed. The depth constraint, the number of layers you can have, is fixed. For the chiplet die itself, you have a good understanding of whether you are going to do this in 2nm or stay with 6nm, but you may have a little bit of room to negotiate that.”
Electrical performance can already be analyzed in the 3D tool, and IR drop, power integrity, thermal, and other multiphysics will be added soon. “At the floor planning level, not only do you get to see electrical performance, but if you change the package material, what happens to signal performance? What happens to power? What happens to thermal? All of that at a floor-planning level should be available to the architect,” Kamdar noted.
Post-training, continuous learning in agentic AI also offers promise for EDA tools to evolve to the needed complexity.
To enable agentic autonomous research, engineers set up research targets and create a benchmark suite. “You kind of cut your agents loose and say, ‘Here’s what I want you to get better at,’” said Jeff Dyck, vice president of R&D at Siemens EDA. [4] “That’s working extremely well for building better tools. It’s in the self-learning theme, and agents are extremely good at this. Then you say, ‘You guys have to build your own models that are better for this.’ Auto fine-tuning, auto distillation, and the like are strong opportunities in that auto-learning space.”
Agentic AI as the foundation for startup solutions
Many startups aim to disrupt traditional EDA tools with a unique selling proposition that leverages AI and/or agents.
“The platform we built is completely scalable for anything — die level, 3D-IC level, and advanced packaging level,” said Solaiman Rahim, chief product officer at ChipAgents. “You can leverage our workflow to solve any kind of problem from chip to system to analog. Then you have to tune the workflow, to make it more advanced, so that your time to results and your cost continue improving, meaning that you can do your advanced packaging in one day instead of taking months. That requires more tuning.”
Fine-tuning of the agentic platform requires strong collaboration with customers. “To achieve this, the customer needs to understand their ontology, their know-how, the way that they are doing certain things,” said Rahim. “The second thing is you need to have both design expertise and domain expertise. Based on that, you can then build some advanced intelligence to tackle those problems. Tuning is building that advanced intelligence, and that advanced intelligence is a brain. You’re actually tuning a brain. We’re not talking about the LLM. We’re talking about a brain sitting in the workflow that is collecting a lot of data, the ontology, and the intelligence of our R&D to solve the customer’s problem and create an algorithm, but that algorithm is much more complex than the traditional algorithm that is capable of taking all this data and working with the LLMs to get to the outcome that you need. That’s what we call the tuning.”
Startup Architect Labs puts proprietary, specialized agents into an end-to-end, full-stack co-design system. “We’re elevating you from an RTL engineer to a human architect,” said Dan Ganousis, head of sales at Architect Labs. “We read the spec and ask, ‘What are you trying to build?’ They say, ‘We’re using a UCIe interface.’ We can go get that. ‘We’re using an Arm core.’ We can go get that and put it in such that the engineer is not writing Verilog to design. He’s writing at the spec level, the architectural level, of what we are trying to accomplish, and then our system takes that, sits on top of all the existing flow, and feeds logic synthesis. We have formal methods that we have customized in our system, so we’re formally verifying as we’re building.”
Another company developed a two-way AI virtual platform, from spec to RTL and from RTL to spec, to enable hardware/software co-design. “With our technology, you give it a spec or model and instead of generating RTL directly, it generates a high-level model, which runs 30´ faster,” said Badru Agarwala, CEO of Rise. “It’s loosely timed. It’s not RTL. Then, using our high-level synthesis tools, you can lower it to RTL. On the other hand, we have other technology that goes from RTL to spec. There, it is the opposite problem. Designers can start verification immediately because these models are timing-dependent. They have all the information, and one advantage of high-level models is that you can explore. If you want to change the memory bandwidth, or you want to change the performance, throughput, timing, 7nm, remove the functionality, all the benefits are available once you have the high-level models to do that.”
Meanwhile, a South Korean startup focuses on a no-code, diagram-first approach to solve power and clock problems in early-stage RTL design. “We make the DFT logic at the RTL design level, so we can shift left the DFT design to the very early stage,” said Jihwan Lee, strategy planning team leader at ITDA. “Our tool is based on a graphical user interface (GUI), so an engineer can just drag and drop the components in our tool and get all the outputs for the synthesis — RTL code and some SDC and UPF for the plug and power synthesis, and DFT tool input file.”
Other companies offer multi-physics simulation tools at extremely high speeds. “There is a crisis in the industry, in my opinion, and the only solution is extremely deep innovation that will give you very high accuracy, but much, much faster,” said Yehea Ismail, co-founder of Suitera, who declined to explain how the high speeds were achieved except that it took seven years.
The shift toward physics-based, AI-enabled tools has proof in the numbers. “A 200-case design sweep that used to take about 16 hours on a legacy thermal workflow now runs in roughly an hour, with setup in under a minute,” said Vinci’s Kabari. “The more telling number, though, is what happens after that. The physics analysis scales near-linearly for runtime inference beyond 10 billion degrees of freedom, because a real system isn’t one component.”
Conclusion
Ultimately, the success of 3D-ICs will depend not only on packaging and process breakthroughs, but also on EDA tools that can keep pace with rapidly changing design requirements. AI tools, machine learning, and agentic systems have value, and there is shared agreement that deterministic physics cannot be left out of the probabilistic AI equation.
From a commercial standpoint, the chip industry consists of EDA, design, and manufacturing. “The technical problem is that these three are still heavily interacting, and so we can see a lot of collaboration,” said Sheng. “If you want to do incremental change [in EDA tools for 3D/HI], each one of these can march forward on its own, but only for a certain amount of time. If you really want non-incremental change, then this has to be done in concert across the three systems. In other words, EDA alone does not optimize what design you can formulate. It’s not that you don’t know what you want. It’s really, can you codify the design and make it programmatic with what you want, and define your boundary conditions in a more disciplined way?”
For now, the physics are not changing. “Light is light, masks are masks,” said Arteris’ Siwinski. “Until we figure out some other way — maybe at some point in the future, there will be some other materials that allow us to make bigger wafers — chiplets are given, 3D packaging is a given, and everything is going to go vertical. Everything needs to be chiplet first, multi-die first, physically-aware first, including package considerations.”
3D is an exciting space. “The fun thing is going to be, will logic dies go the way that memory dies are going?’ Siwinski observed. “Are we really going to start doing 3D logic cubes and rethinking about how packaging is to evolve for that, much more than what’s happening on the memory side? We’ll see.”
— Brendan Heffernan contributed to this report.

articles.title: Meta dégaine 2 nouvelles lunettes connectées Ray-Ban, dont une version sans caméra
articles.text:
Meta continue d’étoffer son catalogue de lunettes connectées. Face au succès de ses précédents modèles, le géant de Menlo Park a dégainé une nouvelle génération de lunettes intelligentes, les Ray-Ban Gen 3 et les Meta Ray-Ban Audio. La firme a décliné ses lunettes sous plusieurs formes, avec pour objectif de proposer « une paire de lunettes pour chaque personnalité ». Plus de 100 modèles différents, réparties entre Ray-Ban, Oakley et Meta Glasses, devraient arriver sur le marché d’ici la fin de l’année.
A lire aussi : On a essayé les Meta VR Glasses, le Vision Pro moins cher et plus léger, en avant-première
Une édition uniquement audio
La première nouveauté est Ray-Ban Meta Audio, la toute première paire de lunettes 100% audio de la marque, sans caméra. Dépourvue d’appareil photo, elle bat un record de légèreté pour Meta. L’offre permet de viser les utilisateurs qui veulent une alternative aux écouteurs Bluetooth et veulent pouvoir converser avec Meta AI sans les questions de vie privée liées à une caméra intégrée. L’audio est « la fonctionnalité la plus populaire des lunettes Meta depuis leurs débuts
 », nous explique Meta.
Côté endurance, la paire offre jusqu’à 12 heures d’autonomie. Les lunettes seront disponibles en précommande dans les styles Burbank et Clubmaster à partir du 23 septembre 2026 au prix de 349 euros. Elles seront sur le marché dès le 13 octobre 2026.
On a pu prendre en main les lunettes à l’issue de la conférence. Dès le premier contact, on a été frappé par la légèreté de la paire. Elle ne pèse que 43 grammes. Les lunettes sont aussi légères et discrètes qu’une paire de lunettes classiques. Impossible de déterminer que vous portez des lunettes Bluetooth, même à une petite distance. Si vous voulez une alternative aux écouteurs, à porter toute la journée au boulot et dans vos activités quotidiennes, c’est peut-être une bonne option, surtout si vous devez porter des lunettes pour votre vue.
A lire aussi : Les lunettes connectées d’Apple veulent éviter le piège des Ray-Ban Meta
Une troisième génération de Ray-Ban
La deuxième annonce de Meta concerne les Ray-Ban Meta de troisième génération, la gamme phare avec caméra et IA embarquée. La génération gagne en finesse, atteint jusqu’à 9 heures d’autonomie (une heure de plus que la Gen2) et intègre un bouton d’action personnalisable pour accéder plus rapidement à Meta AI, ou à une autre fonctionnalité. Le porteur peut choisir lui-même ce que déclenche ce bouton, situé sur la branche droite de la monture. On trouve un bouton analogue sur les lunettes Oakley Meta, dont les fameuses Vanguard, que nous avons testées.
Du reste, la nouvelle génération n’offre rien de particulier en plus par rapport à la seconde mouture. Au moment de la prise en main, on s’est néanmoins rendu compte que l’accessoire était sensiblement plus léger et plus confortable que la Gen 2, auquel nous sommes habitués. Meta nous explique d’ailleurs avoir mis au point de nouvelles charnières ergonomiques et de nouveaux embouts ajustables afin de s’adapter à davantage de morphologies de visage.
Deux nouveaux styles, Aviator et Zena, achèvent la collection, avec une édition limitée Aviator en beige laiteux et verres marron. Cette génération sera disponible dès le 23 septembre 2026 au prix de 449 euros. Du côté des Meta Glasses, lancée il y a quelques semaines sans Ray-Ban, l’entreprise ajoute également deux nouveaux styles, Meta Capri et Meta Nova, disponibles eux aussi à partir du 23 septembre 2026.
Côté logiciel, l’entreprise annonce les « photos dynamiques ». Concrètement, lorsqu’on prend une photo, les lunettes capturent en réalité plusieurs images en une fraction de seconde autour de l’instant où le déclencheur est actionné, puis l’intelligence artificielle de Meta analyse ces prises et sélectionne automatiquement celle qu’elle juge la meilleure. Vous pouvez aussi choisir vous même la photo qui vous plaît le plus. Citons aussi l’arrivée sur toute la gamme d’un mode paysage, et de la capture audio en Dolby Atmos, une première pour ce type de produit.
L’épineuse question de la vie privée
Meta n’a pas hésité à évoquer l’éléphant dans la pièce, à savoir l’épineuse question de la vie privée. De nombreuses personnes se sont en effet servies de l’accessoire pour filmer des individus, surtout des femmes, à leur insu, notamment dans l’espace public.
Comme nous l’a expliqué Meta, une foule de choses ont été mises en place pour éviter ces utilisations abusives des lunettes. Le groupe rappelle avoir intégré une lumière LED, qui s’active quand l’utilisateur filme ou prend une photo. Si cette lumière est masquée, ou trafiquée par l’utilisateur, l’appareil photo ne fonctionnera pas. L’appareil photo va également se désactiver si la LED est couverte pendant l’enregistrement.
« Ce que nous avons observé, c’est que les utilisateurs trouvent des moyens créatifs de contourner ces limites. Nous avons donc mis en place plusieurs mesures ces derniers mois et ces dernières semaines, et je pense que nous avons fait de réels progrès pour comprendre ces comportements, les anticiper et y répondre rapidement », nous relate Meta.
Par ailleurs, Meta se dit conscient que les usagers avec de mauvaises intentions vont continuer de chercher des moyens de contourner les restrictions. C’est pourquoi l’entreprise s’est engagée à prendre des « mesures agressives » à mesure que des abus seront enregistrés. C’est aussi, et surtout, pourquoi Meta décidé de commercialiser des lunettes sans appareil photo.

articles.title: Questionnaire sur l'Australie, site gouvernemental infiltré, mail générique : ce que l'on sait de la nouvelle dérive agentique d'OpenAI
articles.text:
C’est un incident qui date de juin dernier, mais qui vient seulement d’être officialisé.
Le Premier ministre australien Anthony Albanese a révélé le 23 septembre 2026 qu’un agent d’OpenAI avait « infiltré un site web du gouvernement australien » alors qu’il cherchait des statistiques médicales. Le portail concerné héberge des données liées à Medicare, le régime national d’assurance maladie du pays.
OpenAI, de son côté, reconnaît les faits et assure que ses modèles ont agi sans que l’entreprise l’ait voulu.
Des fichiers publics et non publics consultés
Selon la version d’OpenAI, tout est parti d’une évaluation interne. Les modèles de l’entreprise devaient répondre à des questions portant sur l’Australie et ont cherché des réponses et des statistiques sur plusieurs sites et services du gouvernement australien. « Nos modèles ont alors entrepris des actions que nous n’avions pas prévues », explique un porte-parole de l’entreprise au média britannique The Register.
Pour répondre aux interrogations qui lui étaient soumises, l’agent est parti dénicher un accès non autorisé au portail de statistiques de Medicare. D’après Anthony Albanese, des fichiers publics et des fichiers non publics ont été consultés.
Le Premier ministre précise toutefois que ce portail contient des informations « non sensibles », comme des données de dépenses. OpenAI indique pour sa part que l’agent a eu accès à des statistiques de santé agrégées et à des noms de fichiers internes.
Une adresse mail générique pour prévenir Canberra
À ce stade, le gouvernement australien estime qu’aucun autre de ses systèmes n’a été compromis et qu’aucune donnée personnelle n’a été consultée. Deux gouvernements d’États ont toutefois été prévenus que leurs sites avaient aussi été visés, celui d’une agence de lutte contre la criminalité et celui d’un département de la santé.
De son côté, OpenAI dit avoir découvert l’incident en passant en revue les comportements « désalignés » de ses agents et n’a informé Canberra que le 10 septembre. Un délai que l’entreprise justifie par le temps nécessaire pour vérifier les faits mais que le Premier ministre Albanese juge « beaucoup trop long ».
Autre point de colère, la manière dont l’incident a été communiqué. OpenAI se serait en effet contentée d’écrire à l’adresse générique de signalement de l’agence concernée, publicdisclosures@, plutôt qu’à des responsables gouvernementaux.
Présent comme Sam Altman aux réunions des Nations unies, Anthony Albanese dit s’être entretenu avec le patron d’OpenAI pour lui faire part de « l’extrême inquiétude » de l’Australie.

articles.title: „Speicher voll" – der teuerste Hinweis auf deinem Smartphone
articles.text:
Speicher voll? Fünf smarte Wege, das Beste aus deinen Geräten herauszuholen
Schöne neue Welt: Wir teilen Urlaubsfotos noch vor Ort mit Freunden, laden das neue Lieblingsspiel direkt aus dem Store und drehen spontan ein Video in 4K. Dann erscheint plötzlich eine Meldung, die niemand sehen will: „Speicher voll“. Wer besonders knapp an freiem Speicher ist, kann unter Umständen nicht einmal mehr die Kamera oder Messenger-App öffnen. Also beginnt das große Aufräumen: Apps auslagern, alte Videos durchsehen, Screenshots und doppelte Dateien löschen. Das kostet Zeit und Nerven.
Das Problem kommt nicht von ungefähr. Der Datenverbrauch wächst rasant und mit ihm der Bedarf an Speicherplatz.¹ Smartphone-Kameras machen bessere Fotos, die wiederrum mehr Speicherplatz verbrauchen. Eine Minute 4K-Video kann schnell 400 MB belegen.² Aufwendige Spiele füllen mehrere Gigabyte. Gleichzeitig liegen laut einer Bitkom-Studie rund 167 Millionen alte Handys ungenutzt in deutschen Haushalten – viele davon ersetzt, obwohl sie noch funktionierten.³ Dabei lässt sich das Speicherproblem oft einfacher und günstiger lösen als mit einem Neugerät. Die richtigen Speicherlösungen können die Nutzungsdauer von Laptops, Smartphones und Konsolen verlängern.
1. Der Laptop streikt
Für viele ist der Laptop das wichtigste Arbeitsgerät. Speicherprobleme sind hier besonders ärgerlich: Updates bleiben hängen oder lassen sich gar nicht erst herunterladen, Programme starten quälend langsam. Wer kein gutes Ordnungssystem hat, steht beim Löschen von Daten schnell vor einer Mammutaufgabe. Besser also, wenn man sie gleich umgeht: Der SANDISK® Extreme Fit™ USB-C® Flash Drive ist kaum größer als eine Fingerkuppe, sodass er dauerhaft im USB-C-Anschluss stecken bleiben kann – ganz nach dem Prinzip „Plug & Stay“. Die kompakte Bauform geht nicht zulasten der Kapazität: Der Flash Drive bietet bis zu 1 TB Speicherplatz.⁴ Mit Lesegeschwindigkeiten von bis zu 400 MB/s⁵ lassen sich Dateien schnell übertragen und sind ganz ohne Cloud oder stabile Internetverbindung jederzeit zugänglich.
2. Das iPhone® absichern
Noch intensiver nutzen viele ihr Smartphone. Fotos und Videos konkurrieren mit Apps, Podcasts und Musikdateien um den verfügbaren Speicherplatz. Ist dann auch die Cloud voll, braucht es eine unkomplizierte Lösung für Backups. Schließlich schließen nur wenige ihr Handy regelmäßig an den Laptop an. Der SANDISK Phone Drive für iPhone® schafft Abhilfe. Nutzer können den Stick einfach ans iPhone anschließen und Fotos, Videos oder andere Backups mit bis zu 90 MB/s übertragen. Mit bis zu 256 GB¹ Kapazität bietet der Stick reichlich Platz für wichtige Daten.
3. Die Spielebibliothek wächst und wächst
Auch Videospiele verlangen immer mehr Speicherplatz. Die Spielwelten werden komplexer, die Dateien größer. Das Action-Game Split Fiction benötigt beispielsweise mehr als 70 GB. Da ist der interne Speicher der Handheld-Konsole schnell gefüllt. Wer Spiele nicht ständig auslagern und neu herunterladen möchte, kann sein Gaming-Setup mit der SANDISK GamePlay microSD™ Express-Karte um bis zu 512 GB erweitern. Die Karte erreicht Übertragungsgeschwindigkeiten von bis zu 880 MB/s.⁶ Dadurch verkürzen sich Ladezeiten und Spiele laufen flüssiger.
4. Unterwegs arbeiten, ohne Daten zu riskieren
Auf Reisen entstehen schnell große Datenmengen: Fotos und Videos von Stadtrundgängen, vom Strand oder aus den Bergen. Wer unterwegs noch arbeitet, füllt den Gerätespeicher im Handumdrehen. Gerade wenn nicht immer stabiles Internet verfügbar ist. Dabei sollen Bilder und Videos gesichert und jederzeit verfügbar bleiben – ob im Zug, im Hotel oder am Flughafen. Hier kommt die SANDISK Extreme® Portable SSD ins Spiel. Sie bietet bis zu 4 TB¹ Speicherplatz im kompakten Format. Mit Lesegeschwindigkeiten von bis zu 2.000 MB/s² lassen sich beispielsweise 1.000 hochauflösende Fotos in weniger als einer Minute⁷ übertragen. Die portable SSD ist gegen Wasser, Staub und Stürze aus bis zu drei Metern⁸ geschützt. Der Passwortschutz sowie die Hardwareverschlüsselung sorgen zudem dafür, dass die Daten noch sicherer bleiben – selbst wenn das Laufwerk verloren geht oder gestohlen wird.⁹
5. Überall Content drehen, schneiden und posten
Guter Content ist oft nicht geplant. In inspirierenden Momenten heißt es: Handy zücken und aufnehmen. Damit das Smartphone auch bei längeren hochauflösenden Videos mithält, braucht es eine Lösung, die direkt am Gerät sitzt, große Dateien speichert, wenn der interne Speicher schnell an seine Grenzen kommt, und einen reibungslosen Workflow ermöglicht. Hier kommt die SANDISK Creator Phone SSD ins Spiel. Sie lässt sich magnetisch an MagSafe®-kompatiblen Smartphones befestigen und speichert Aufnahmen direkt auf dem Laufwerk. Auf kompatiblen iPhones lassen sich auch Apple ProRes®-Videoaufnahmen in 4K mit 60 Bildern pro Sekunde speichern. Nach dem Dreh können die Dateien unmittelbar weiterbearbeitet werden. Das Silikongehäuse, der IP65-Schutz und der Fallschutz aus bis zu drei Metern Höhe⁸ machen die SSD zu einer robusten Begleiterin für mobile Drehs. Dank exFAT-Formatierung funktioniert sie mit Windows®, Android®, macOS® und iOS®.
Fazit: Mehr Platz, weniger Frust
Mangelnder Speicherplatz sollte nur selten ein Grund sein, ein funktionierendes Gerät zu ersetzen. Ob am Laptop im Büro, mit dem Smartphone im Urlaub, beim Gaming auf der Couch oder beim Dreh auf der Straße: Mit der passenden Speicherlösung von Sandisk lässt sich mehr aus vorhandener Hardware herausholen. So bleibt der Kopf frei für das, was wirklich zählt: Erinnerungen festhalten, neue Highscores und kreative Meilensteine erreichen.

articles.title: Tapez juste « @ » : cette nouvelle fonction cachée de Google Docs va complètement révolutionner la rédaction d'un document
articles.text:
L’IA Gemini de Google est partout. Notamment dans la suite bureautique en ligne de la firme, intégrant Docs, Slides et Sheets, entre autres. Par exemple pour générer des images ou des graphiques à partir de votre texte.
De la même manière, vous pouvez demander à Gemini de regarder dans vos autres services Google (Drive, Gmail…), ou encore le Web, pour rédiger un document en lien avec les données que l’IA y trouve. À côté, il y a Gemini Notebook, anciennement NotebookLM.
iPhone 18 Pro à 99€ + forfait 250Go à 29,99€/mois pendant 12 mois. Profitez de 50€ de remise immédiate avec le code NEW50 et jusqu’à 150€ de bonus reprise pour votre ancien mobile. Livraison offerte.
Alors que l’outil est précisément là pour réunir vos notes et sources de recherche sur un sujet donné à l’aide de l’IA, il restait jusqu’ici à l’écart de Docs. Google vient d’annoncer son intégration dans le traitement de texte.
Gemini Notebook s’invite dans Google Docs, l’IA peut s’en servir comme source
En clair, quand vous saisissez votre requête dans le champ dédié à Gemini, en bas d’un Docs ou dans le panneau latéral, vous pouvez appuyer sur la touche « @ » puis taper le nom d’un de vos « notebooks ». Il apparaît alors dans la liste des sources proposées. Gemini s’appuie alors sur ses sources pour rédiger ce que vous lui avez demandé.
Plus besoin de garder vos notebooks ouverts dans un autre onglet pour vérifier que le texte rédigé par Gemini ne raconte pas n’importe quoi. Gemini ajoute en effet dans le texte des citations tirées des sources du notebook, avec un lien pour les consulter.
L’option est disponible depuis ce mercredi 23 septembre, sans déploiement progressif. Pour en profiter, il faut une formule Google Workspace Business Standard ou Plus, Enterprise Standard ou Plus, ou Education Plus, avec les fonctions intelligentes de Workspace activées.
En tant que particulier, il vous faut un abonnement à Google AI Pro (21,99 euros par mois) ou Ultra (à partir de 99,99 euros par mois). La formule d’entrée Google AI Plus, à 4,99 euros par mois, ne donne pas accès à cette fonction.
